maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister);
maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my sad duty to announce to members of the house the death this morning of a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council, General A. G. L. McNaughton, after a career of continuous service to his country in war and peace, service of the greatest distinction, extending over more than 60 years.
The value to his country of General McNaughton's services was equalled only by the courage and unselfishness he always showed in performing those services. On the military side perhaps he was best known as the first commander of Canada's First Army overseas, and for the magnificent way in which he prepared that army for the great part it was to play in the liberation of Europe.
After the war, when General McNaughton had so richly earned rest and retirement, his activities if anything increased. Among other things he represented Canada very ably at the United Nations when our country was first elected to the security council. He also served with distinction for many years as chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission.
General McNaughton was always active and vigorous in public affairs, right up to the day of his death, especially in promoting what he considered to be right policies in the preservation and the development of our natural resources. In a very real sense he died in action and he would never have had it any other way. My own friendship with General McNaughton, which I shall always cherish, goes back for many years. He was a warm hearted, whole souled and high minded gentleman.
There was nothing mean or small about nim, but much that was brave and good and wise. Canada has lost one of its most distinguished sons. I send my deepest sympathy to Mrs. McNaughton and the members of the family.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR
speechtext:
I join with the Prime Minister in the expression of sympathy to General McNaughton's widow and the members of his family. He served his country in many capacities. During the first world war he gave distinguished service and through his initiative brought about changes in artillery warfare which are still being followed today. After the war he resumed his position in the scientific world and gave of his best.
During the period between the first and second world wars he continued to take an interest in the armed forces, and then took the Canadian army overseas. The circumstances in which he ceased to command that army in action will be for historians to determine. The Prime Minister mentioned the fact that he was a member of the Privy Council of Canada. I well recall the circumstances in which he assumed the position of minister of defence in succession to Colonel Ralston. During the period of his life in active politics he took stands which were not generally acceptable, but he was able to do so because of the great respect he had built up in the years of service to his country. I believe that when history writes the story of his life it will be said of him that, while he served well in many capacities, and combined as it were, two careers, that of science and that of the military, his outstanding contribution was his devotion to Canada in connection with those matters which came under his jurisdiction as the chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission.
To his widow and his family the condolences of this house will be conveyed. This was a Canadian who in his day and generation, whatever the differences and the difficulties may have been, followed the course that he determined was for the benefit of Canada.

maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR
speechtext:
The members of the New Democratic Party desire to join hon. members of all parties in paying tribute to General McNaughton and the very great services which he has rendered to this country. As hon. members know, he was born in Moosomin, Saskatchewan, and the people of that province always looked

Tributes to General A. G. L. McNaughton upon him as one of their native sons who earned great distinction. They will always remember him with great pride.
As the commander of the Canadian army in the second world war he won the esteem and affection of the men who served under him. As minister of defence he gave this country great leadership. I owed a personal debt to him because while he held that office he arranged for me to visit Saskatchewan personnel overseas, and I shall never forget his many kindnesses to me on that occasion.
In the field of science, as head of the research council, he did valuable work for his country. As chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission I for one can testify to the effective way in which he upheld Canada's rights on the commission. I remember one or two disputes we had about conserving Canadian water, which was a very scarce commodity on the prairies, and because of the battle which he put up so effectively we were able to carry out programs which otherwise would have been impossible.
However, I think his most distinguished feature was that as he grew older in years he remained eternally young in spirit. In recent years he became the chief proponent in Canada of policies for the conservation of Canada's water resources, and while for a time it seemed he was a voice crying in the wilderness I think the aroused public interest in this question today is a credit to his tenacity and his foresight.
I am sure members in all parties in the house will want to join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, in conveying to Mrs. McNaughton, and the members of the General's family our deepest sympathy, along with an expression of our pride in one of the great Canadians of our generation.

maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, General McNaughton was unquestionably a great and, in every way, a distinguished Canadian.
The members of the Ralliement Creditiste join the right hon. Prime Minister in offering Mrs. McNaughton and her family their deepest sympathy. Many Canadians considered the general as their hero, and I am sure all of Canada mourns this great loss to the country.

maintopic: GENERAL A. G. L. McNAUGHTON TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF LATE PRIVY COUNCILLOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that we all share a feeling of loss at the death of General McNaughton as we join in the expressions of sympathy that have been uttered by the right hon. Prime Minister and the other party leaders in the house. He was indeed a great soldier, a statesman, a scientist, a humanitarian, a Canadian of tireless energy and great intellectual capacity.
But what is more important, Mr. Speaker, is that in this day of conformity he dared to be an individualist. He held strong opinions and expressed them clearly and forcefully without waiting first to see which way the political wind was blowing. Those who knew him well and worked with him will remember his warm personality and will remember him as one whose insight into the needs of his country and whose powers of persuasion played a great role in preserving our national status.
General McNaughton never let the problems of a situation or the fatigue of advanced years thwart him from the duty at hand. Even after he had retired he continued to take an active role in public affairs. We sometimes had occasion to disagree with him, but we always respected him as a sagacious gentleman.
Historians will discuss his views for many years to come. His opinions on the second world war, his statements on the cold war, on our relationship with the United States, on our national water resources and on a host of other subjects will form the basis of many a learned debate. One thing is certain; he had the courage of his convictions and the more people we have like him the better off we will be. Canada has lost a great and devoted servant. Our deepest sympathy is extended to Mrs. McNaughton and the family, whose grief the nation shares.

speechtext:
It will be recalled that the
statute passed in 1964 authorizes loans to be made to students who are certified by the appropriate authority in each participating province to be in need of a loan of a specified amount. The provincial governments have co-operated by designating such authorities in their provinces, thereby enabling our legislation to be effective. They have also integrated it in varying degrees with their own student aid programs which include many bursaries awarded after a careful appraisal of the needs of the various applicants.
The provincial authorities have felt, and we have agreed, that we should strive for as much consistency as possible among participating provinces in the practices and standards they apply in administering this program, recognizing, of course, the need for some flexibility to allow for special circumstances and conditions. With this in mind we have encouraged and assisted provincial representatives to meet together periodically, and representatives of the Department of Finance have met with them. We have recognized that under our legislation the provincial authorities have the authority and responsibility for determining the relative need of the various applicants for student loans and thereby ensuring a fair apportionment among students of the amount of guaranteed loans which parliament has authorized.
In view of the terms of our legislation all of us, the provinces and the federal government, have proceeded on the general basis that need must be taken into account, and we have endeavoured to co-ordinate and work out with the provinces sensible principles to be observed in doing this. The agreed principles are expressed in the report I have tabled.

speechtext:
1.	Are there any payments overdue to the city of Halifax on behalf of the National Harbours Board, the Canadian National Railways, and other government agencies, in lieu of taxes for each of the past 3 years and the present year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of State):
subtopic: HALIFAX-OVERDUE PAYMENTS IN LIEU OF TAXES
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Finance and Transport as follows:
Questions
1.	Payments in lieu of taxes are ex gratia in nature and cannot be described as overdue inasmuch as no legal liability has been incurred in respect of them. The various federal agencies operating in Halifax do pay annual grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities. Efforts are made to have the payments effected during the financial year of the municipality to which they relate. However, it is not always possible to settle grants before the end of the municipality's financial year. In the city of Halifax, the amounts of the grants in respect of 1965 and 1966 have not yet been finally determined or paid by one agency, i.e., the National Harbours Board. Payments in respect of 1964 and 1963 have been settled in all instances.
2.	The payment of grants in lieu of taxes in so far as the National Harbours Board is concerned for the calendar years 1965 and 1966 have been delayed due to the time required to determine the amounts payable under a new formula which increases the grants. However, an interim payment for the year 1965 has been made in the amount of $148,350 to the city of Halifax and the remainder will be paid as soon as the necessary assessment values and calculations have been determined to fix the exact amount of the grant. All grants have been made up to and including 1964 and an interim payment for the year 1965.

Has a request been received by the federal government, or the Atlantic Development Board, from

Mr. Speaker, I would direct a question to the Minister of Transport. I ask that question in view of the fact that those of us sitting on this side of the house have, I think without exception, taken a strong stand against any increase, which will have a serious and detrimental effect on Canada.

I think this is a wholly responsible attitude on our part, and I am sure the right hon. gentleman would have taken it had he been on this side of the house.
Any change in tolls will not come into effect before the opening of navigation in 1967, and I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that no action will be taken by the government until an announcement is made in this house.
I think it is very important that an announcement be made, that the government should take whatever responsibility it is required to take, and that the house should hold the government responsible for doing so. At the same time let me point out that the right hon. gentleman was in this house, although I was not, when the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act was passed, so he knows perfectly well-and I am sure he was one of those who supported it-that that act requires the government and the seaway authority to impose a level of tolls which will amortize that investment. The house in committee of supply, Mr. Batten in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, picking up the threads of the debate of last Friday afternoon, we come back to the question of Canada's role and policy in the Viet Nam war. As a premise to my remarks on the situation in Viet Nam I should first like to commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his diplomatic efforts to date, particularly in the light of some of the unwarranted criticism directed at him last Friday afternoon by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
The hon. member attacked the minister for not entering with full speed into what the hon. member termed the new age of diplomacy. He was even contemptuous of the minister's efforts to work behind the scenes and use whatever influence Canada may have as constructively as possible. I am surprised that one with the experience of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam could possibly entertain the belief that world diplomacy has suddenly become some sort of mass participation sport, the players' moves being determined by the effective rhetoric of other participants.
The hon. member seems to envisage international relations as entering an era when the assembling of world opinion will serve as
July 11. 1966



the principal generative force. The hon. member is suggesting that everything be made public. Mobilize world opinion and pressure the major powers into a settlement which the hon. member and world opinion consider satisfactory. It seems to me that the hon. member is forgetting that so-called world opinion is little more than those who, by sheer audacity, seek to establish themselves as the spokesmen for the world community. The hon. member went to great pains to mention the Prime Minister of India, the junior senator from New York, and the senior senators from Montana and Arkansas. Presumably he feels that they, along with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam himself, constitute world opinion.
Moreover, the hon. member is entertaining a fancy, which it may be noted is fine as long as one is not vested with responsibility, an illusion that even if he, the junior senator from New York and the rest of "world opinion" did have valid claims, they would in any way be able to orient the foreign policy of any belligerent in this conflict, let alone the major powers concerned. Were these heralds of world opinion able to change the policy of the Soviet Union at the time of the Hungarian crisis? As I think back I wonder if they even tried. Admittedly no nation enjoys a poor press review, but nations cannot afford to compromise their own interest for the sake of those who, from a different vantage point, may not agree with them. No better example of this point can be had than the present policy and the attitude of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
It must also be noted that over-publication of diplomacy serves only to polarize positions and to make compromise that much more difficult. This the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam seemed to forget when he deprecated the efforts of the minister to work behind the scenes through the Ronning missions and other endeavours as well. If my memory serves me accurately, Mr. Chairman, the most valuable achievements in international relations occur behind closed doors where all the factors are considered and where rigid positions can be modified with proper and less embarassing bargaining.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, like other hon. members, does not have possession of all the facts in relation to the Viet Nam war. We are not in a position to weigh all the variables and to consider all the factors as only the responsible, who are intimately involved, are able to do. No member 23033-4731
Interim. Supply
of this house has access to all the information which comes to the minister, and such must be the case.
Another thing which must be understood is that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam does not have responsibility for the difficult decisions that have to be made regarding Viet Nam. For him to assume the posture of castigating so vehemently the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the President of the United States and, by implication, the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand, when he is in possession of only a fraction of the information, seems to me to be highly presumptuous.
Moreover, we must recognize that Canada as a middle power is quite limited in what she may be able to achieve. It has been demanded that Canada insist that the Geneva conference be reconvened and that the United States halt the bombing of North Vietnamese military targets. But recognizing the hon. member's oratorical gifts it would not have been surprising had he demanded that Canada should flood the world for 40 days and 40 nights if the Canadian demands were not met. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, we cannot afford to minimize the honourable influence which we can have in the world community, but we cannot expect the Secretary of State for External Affairs or anyone else, including the Secretary General of the United Nations, to perform miracles in the present difficult international situation.
No, Mr. Chairman, I think we must understand that international politics are not some sort of world parlour game. We recognize the fact that weighty decisions can only be made by a few, and that the potential for successful diplomacy is best behind the closed door. Therefore, while we in this party do not always agree with the government and its emphasis in the Viet Nam conflict, we would not have the Secretary of State for External Affairs preaching from the rooftops or conducting his efforts in any other manner than he has already done during these last few months with respect to the realities of the Viet Nam problem.
In the light of the platitudes and hyperboles inflicted upon this chamber last Friday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I wish to take note of some of the considerations which to this point have been ignored. What has always disturbed me about the position assumed by some hon. members is the naive view that in international relations we are to consider first and foremost certain

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
moral standards and that considerations of power and self-interest are to have no place. I wish that that were true. According to these hon. members policy has to be determined by a just formula; all that is required is a gentleman's agreement and good faith on the part of all and everything will work out quite satisfactorily.
Unfortunately, however, man is not to be so easily trusted, and a nation's policy, regardless of the moral explanations given to the contrary, is based on the safeguarding of the nation's interest and the defence of its strategic position in the world power structure. We have not yet entered the era when the brotherhood of man makes any just solution viable in itself. I wish we had.
The hon. member seems to refuse to recognize the facts of geopolitics and to confront the implications of the alarming changes in the power structure of Asia. I can understand that he may say, "Is peace not worth attempting at all?" Of course it is. But the only peace we can realistically hope for is that condition wherein the aggressive power considers further expansion as more of a loss than the sacrifice of old dreams and ambitions. It is well that we remember that in Southeast Asia the expanding power is China and the containing power is the United States with its allies.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is impossible, Mr. Chairman, to view the events in Viet Nam apart from the situation in Asia as a whole and particularly the rejuvenation of China as a major world power. Surely this is the ultimate consideration here. Can the revival of a Chinese empire extending to the South China seas and perhaps farther be contained? There is no doubt that the revolutionaries under Chairman Mao differ little in aim and intent from the Ming dynasty. There are those who suggest that the west should retreat from the mainland of Asia altogether and set the line of containment at Australasia, Japan and the Philippines. In the view of this school, mainland Asia would be recognized as the Chinese sphere of influence.
Ignoring for just a moment the injustice of abandoning so many peoples whose history has been characterized by their hostility to Chinese domination, let us consider such a solution purely as it relates to strategy. Could the west successfully defend the above-mentioned areas against a China economically inoculated with the acquisition of rich new fields to the south? Such a Chinese empire

with a sophisticated nuclear delivery system, a burgeoning population demanding new food areas, would look covetously to the vast plains of Australia. The potential for economic warfare alone against Australia is frightening inasmuch as China would have control over most of the major trade routes in the area.
Another suggestion has been the possibility of a Titoist formula for Viet Nam. It is argued that considering the historical hatred of the Vietnamese people for the Chinese, it is quite probable that we would witness the evolution of a national Communist state in Viet Nam which would be able to resist the grander designs of China. Such a solution, however, does not take into account the fact that the anti-Chinese element in the North Vietnamese government is restricted to President Ho Chi-Minh and the old veterans of the party. The young Turk movement represented by such energetic figures as General Vo Nguyen Giap is quite proChinese and see their country's future as linked to that of China. Moreover, the success of the Chinese policy as formulated by Mao-Tse-Tung and Marshal Lin Piao, that is, the use of the war of national liberation, as opposed to the Soviet view, could only strengthen the position of China in the Communist movement in Viet Nam and indeed throughout Asia.
It is highly unlikely then, with the eventual emergence of the pro-Chinese movement in the North Vietnamese Communist party and with the obvious success of the Chinese formula, that a Titoist Viet Nam could exist without the limits of sovereignty being set by the Chinese. Moreover, with the removal of the United States and the absence of an Asian counter-force to Chinese power, a nationalist regime would have much difficulty in pursuing an independent line which was liable on occasion to be to the detriment of the Chinese. For the Soviet union to counter Chinese power in Southern Asia is even more impractical than the United States, for the latter is at least a Pacific power. Her borders extend deep into the Pacific and her ultimate interest in Australia makes her very deeply involved in the Asian situation. The Soviet Union on the other hand is a European power and is becoming increasingly oriented to Europe. Granted, the Soviet union is the logical power to meet Chinese expansion in the north but she does not have the geopolitical resources to counter Chinese expansion in the south.
July 11. 1966

This is not to mention the problems which would be posed for the neighbouring states should Viet Nam come under Chinese domination, subtle and indirect though it may appear. For the moment the combined forces of the neutralists under Prince Souvanna Phouma and the pro-western elements in Laos have been able to contain the advances of the Pathet Lao which has been largely ignored by their patrons in North Vietnam, who have been almost totally preoccupied with the war in the south. With a united Viet Nam under Ho Chi-Minh to what extent could the Laotian government further resist the incursions of the Pathet Lao? What about the situation in Thailand and Cambodia? Would not those countries be forced to seek accommodation with China, an accommodation which would be politically and economically advantageous to the Chinese. In fact it is not unreasonable to suggest that Prince Sihanouk has already opted for the Chinese, expecting them to have eventual control over Indochina. One must also ask whether the integrity of Malaysia and Singapore could be guaranteed and whether Indonesian General Suharto and his supporters could continue to steer that country toward truly national development.
All of this is ignoring one of the basic facts of this struggle and that is the question of United States prestige. Even were the difficulties posed by withdrawal to be overcome, it is not to be expected that the United States will follow the suggestions made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, suggestions which, it may be noted, are tantamount to complete capitulation. Already some Europeans see the struggle of conscience in the United States as evidence that that country's guarantees are not to be trusted in the long run. Free nations everywhere could no longer count on American assistance against aggression from a more powerful nation. To expect the United States to unconditionally stop the bombing and to withdraw without a like action from the North Vietnamese is highly unrealistic and quite impossible.
Chinese imperialism is no less imperialistic for being in the guise of insurgency. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is quick to accept the claims of that minority which always claims to speak for the majority. Therefore I would ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam if he would suggest that the attempted coup last October in Indonesia, in which the Chinese were deeply involved, was a true expression of Indonesian feeling?
Interim Supply
Yes, we have been warned of an impending nuclear holocaust, of greater participation from the Communist world. We have been told so often that the United States is forcing the Russians and the Chinese together, and yet Sino-Soviet relations are at a worse point now than they have ever been. The dangers of east European volunteers pose no major threat as the mobility and supply of such volunteers would be almost impossible under the circumstances.
There has been a great deal spoken of American atrocities, about women and children being bombed and maimed. Nothing has been said about the atrocities on the Viet Nam side. The same people who criticize in this regard and who do not recognize the truth in the statement might read some of the reports which contain the views of Canadian members of the international control commission team. All we need do is read the minority report to understand that.
It has been the Vietcong which has systematically attacked the civilian population, bombed city restaurants, murdered village leaders and tortured those who refused to co-operate. The hon. member talks about reform. Every time an attempt is made to provide a village with trained officials they are assassinated by the Vietcong. True economic reforms would be realized sooner if the Vietcong did not consistently sabotage Vietnamese villages and did not execute such a systematic terrorism over the civilian population. The hon. member would find that refugees from Vietcong areas, not to mention the more than one million refugees from North Vietnam who fled from Communism into South Vietnam when the Geneva agreement was established, could certainly give him a graphic picture of Vietcong atrocities.
Over the weekend I noticed an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of July 1. I believe it is worth taking note of and worth putting on the record in part at least. It reads:
Britain, Canada, the U.S.S.R., the secretary general of the UN and others, have made many efforts to bring Hanoi to the conference table. The Americans have made it clear beyond any reasonable doubt that they are willing to talk. The Chinese have released the terms of approaches the Americans have made, including token withdrawals of troops, to save face for the North Vietnamese government. All these approaches have been rejected. All would-be mediators have insisted that a necessary pre-condition of negotiation is the cessation of bombing. U Thant continues to offer this argument. The Americans discontinued bombing for six weeks and a major peace effort was made during that period. Hanoi rejected every overture. The cessation of bombing had no effect. The proposition that the

central committee, and also to embark on a workable reform program in the rural areas. This is something we are told very little about.
There have been increasing provisions by the administration for medical care, agricultural assistance, educational facilities in a country ravaged by war. The Viet Cong are relying less on their division size operations and have returned to hit and run attacks. One thing is becoming clear. The Communists cannot win the war militarily. There is only one hope for them of victory and that is for weariness to set in upon the allies in response to those who insist they should withdraw as they cannot win. Unfortunately for many of these their efforts have not been too successful. These voices which call for withdrawal are the same voices which said of Greece after the war that the Communists spoke for the majority and that their victory in Greece was inevitable.
I would say that while we do not like the developments and we do not like to talk about war the fact is that the situation in Viet Nam is beginning to change and that China is being contained. Prime Minister Sato of Japan said only last week:
It is my earnest hope that the United States will continue to persevere in its efforts toward stability and peace in Viet Nam.
He was paying tribute to the U.S. military role in Asia. The views of Prime Minister Holt of Australia, Prime Minister Tungku Abdul Rhahman of Malaysia and Prime Minister Keith Holyoake of New Zealand are all well known.
We come to this point as we consider the war in Viet Nam. This is not just a United States war as we would be led to believe by some. This is an allied effort involving the troops of South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines, and the non-combat assistance of many other countries. The nations on China's periphery are understandably concerned and are determined that Chinese expansion be contained. As Coral Belle, the well known Australian strategist, put it:
They tell us China is a long way from Australia but Japan was a long way from Australia too.
As Mr. Patrick Gordon-Walker noted when he was in Toronto at the international teach-in, and as Mr. Enoch Powell has noted since, the United States is a Pacific power which must now lead this alliance. When an Asian power structure does emerge to balance that
Interim Supply
of China, the United States can consider withdrawal from southeast Asia. That time is not now.
I should like to conclude with a word about Canada's role in this struggle. There are some who feel that Canada's position on the International Control Commission gives her a certain neutrality in the situation. There is some justice in the argument that Canada's role in the I.C.C. may be such that active military participation would be unwise and would tend to cripple any influence we might have in that body. I would agree with that. However, as a commonwealth nation historically linked to Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, and as an ally of the United States, we cannot be completely neutral. The International Control Commission role does not demand this. Poland, for instance is also a member of the I.C.C. and yet that country last week offered volunteers for the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese. It is in this area that I feel the government deserves some criticism. There is no reason why Canada cannot substantially increase her aid to South Viet Nam. We are contributing only about $1 million, which in this case is a trifling amount.
As the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said, United States citizens in Viet Nam are dying for you and me. Even if we cannot send troops there is no reason why we cannot increase our economic assistance. There is a tremendous need so that the reform programs in the rural areas can work and so that South Viet Nam will eventually become a peaceful, stable and prosperous nation. Surely there is no member in this house who would oppose such a development. It has been long argued that the war cannot be won by military means alone. I refer again to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but I would be the first to agree with those remarks and I hope that the hon. member and everyone else in this house would support an effort to increase our economic assistance to that war-torn country. We hope the government will make a real attempt to correct this situation. We appreciate the diplomatic conduct of the minister, although I cannot agree that the government cannot do more than what is presently being done.
While it is necessary that we must continue to explore that diplomatic role which is uniquely ours, and while we feel that Canada should continue the liaison role she has been playing, facilitating in many ways the exchange of positions, we cannot help but feel

July 11. 1966
Interim Supply
nevertheless that Canada must remain sympathetic to the allied struggle in Viet Nam, supporting our friends and allies as they attempt to preserve the national integrity and independence of Asian nations from the indirect but very aggressive force to the north which says its foreign policy is to take part in all revolutionary wars such as those which have been recently so prevalent in many parts of the world. There is no better current example of this than Indonesia.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It would seem to me that in addition to this position which I think Canada can take through a greater and expanding role in a humanitarian contribution to the world picture, we have to face up to the fact that the only hope we have today for peace in Asia is a containment of the warlike, aggressive policies of China, even as Russia 15 years ago was contained through the effect of NATO.
This being so, and with the passing of time, I am sure that many of the critical situations which today seem to have no solution will ease up and provide an opportunity for the integrity and autonomy of nations in the eastern part of the world. This can play a very decided role in the over-all developing pattern toward the goal which we all share, which is the peaceful development of the world's resources.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that I find myself at considerable variance with much of what was said by the hon. member for Red Deer. I find it somewhat peculiar that in this country where we believe in democracy, where we consider ourselves a Christian nation, where we have subscribed to the ideals and the charter of the United Nations, we should hear the leader of a political party as much as say that we should have no part in idealism, that when we consider the world of today we should consider it in the light of cold, ruthless, power politics and that is the only thing that counts. The hon. member used such arguments as: What do they think about Hungary when they talk about atrocities or taking over countries by subversion, force of arms, etc? It is no argument, I submit, when ever a question of the legality of anyone's actions is concerned, to say that the action taken in Hungary was not legal. Where does that leave us? I presume from the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer that once the Communists have done it this brings such action to an acceptable level.
The hon. member used the same argument about atrocities. I gathered from his remarks

that he is perfectly happy about atrocities. Because one side is guilty of atrocities, he seems to think this makes atrocities the sort of thing we should favour. I am sure that the conscience and the mind of every citizen in this country who pays more than lip service to those ideals by which we profess to live, and which we hope will even guide relations between states, are more than a little perturbed at the thought of the number of innocent men, women and children who are today dying or suffering because of the conflict in Viet Nam.
I believe that those who are Christians and those who say that people in other countries should be able to enjoy the same rights and privileges that we do are a little aghast at the argument of the hon. member for Red Deer that the people in that country do not count because their country is just a pawn and its people mere ciphers in a power struggle between China and the mighty United States which cannot be stopped.
Surely there is more to our world than that. Surely these people are more than ciphers who can be swatted like flies by contending giants. I for one do not subscribe to the idea that the ends justify the means, as was so vehemently exhorted by the hon. member. It does seem to me that there is a right way and a wrong way to do things. It does seem to me that today, when the contending ideologies of our version of democracy and communism are in a struggle, we do nothing to help the cause of democracy by abandoning the very ideals that make our way of life so worth while for us.
I am not at all convinced that the United States, by saying that the ends justify the means, is achieving those ends which alone could justify the means, if they are not indeed acting illegally. I would like to see the argument in this house conducted along the line of those who contend that the United States is right in standing up and proving what right the United States has to be there. I have heard no one pretend that the United States has any right other than might.
I am a little concerned when we so far abandon even any pretence at legality, when we ignore the question of the means of achieving an objective and then are not even sure of the objective. This is no way for democracy to win any struggle, short or long term. It is my contention that by abondoning our ideals every new, emerging or underdeveloped country in this world that we might hope to convert to our system of democracy is going to find that we in the
July 11. 1966

western world are a bunch of hypocrites when we talk of democracy, that we in the western world do not believe in the United Nations charter which we signed and which gives each country equal rights.
There is nothing in our present attitude toward Viet Nam which can do anything but convince small nations around the world that they are meaningless as nations, that the lives of their citizens mean nothing to us, and that we do not subscribe to any of our ideals that we so proudly proclaim as being the hallmark of democracy. I do not know how we in this house can say that our objectives are to contain communism and in the same breath go along with the very type of action for which we say we hate and fear communism.

With a middle power such as Canada which enjoys membership on the International Control Commission and has had an unparalleled measure of success in contributing to solutions of international disputes, and with a Secretary of State for External Affairs-I do not say this because I am a Liberal member- who has a record of acceptability, if you like, putting it in its most undramatic terms, is it not in this area that this country can serve its most useful purpose? If it is not, then I should like to hear suggestions to the contrary from the other side. I do not think it is useful to tell us we should be making certain statements while we are attempting to negotiate. Negotiations never have been aided and abetted by such pronouncements by the third party. The third party role is an undramatic role by definition; it is a role which demands a tremendous amount of patience, perseverance, tact and imagination. It is not a role that can be built up as a role which will excite the fancies of those who read the newspapers around the country and across the world. It is an undramatic but important role.
I think what should be coming out of this debate is an assessment of the particular role which has been created by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would be very interested to hear from hon. members on the other side how this particular role may be improved and refined. I think if we had that we might have a meaningful debate in this house rather than the sort of thing we have been having up until now. My position in this matter is simply that I prefer our present role for a middle power such as ours with our record. It seems to me it is the only hopeful approach which we, this government, and in fact this country can take in trying to serve some purpose in bringing to an end what we all regard as a very tragic war.

Mr. Chairman, in listening to the speech of the hon. member for Peterborough I was very interested in his constant reiterations about negotiations. He did not tell us with whom the negotiations are taking place. One can only assume he meant that our government was in the process of negotiating with the United States. If that is the case, then I am unable to understand why he still
Interim Supply
has some hope for the success of those negotiations. I would have hoped that each member of this Canadian parliament would have reacted very adversely to the treatment of the Prime Minister of Canada received at the hands of the President of the United States when he sought to place before the American people and the American government Canada's great concern about the escalation of the war. The reaction was a prompt and almost immediate escalation by the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong. How many more times do we have to be kicked in the teeth before we realize that this kind of diplomacy just is not working?
I remember some months ago speaking to a member of the United States Congress. I asked him whether he thought it would have any effect upon the policies of the United States government if the spokesmen of the Canadian government were, plainly and bluntly from their seats in the House of Commons, to express their real dismay at and opposition to the present United States policy in South Viet Nam. This congressman told me that he could not answer that question but that he could tell me something else. He said it in these words; I can tell you that the present attitude of your government in Canada is being used today by our President to beat down the opposition to his policies in the United States Senate and the United States House of Representatives. This in effect, of course, was a suggestion that there is some effect.
I was very doubtful, Mr. Chairman, whether I would enter this debate until I heard the truly shocking speech of the hon. member for Red Deer. I found it particularly shocking, coming from someone who, shall we say, makes a very open profession of Christian principles, to find that he has become enamoured of the German pre-war theory of realpolitik which subordinates all other considerations to the advancement of the state in various parts of the world. I suppose it is hardly necessary to recite the horrors of the war in southeast Asia. The Secretary General of the United Nations, U Thant, already has described it in his view as the most horrible war in history. I think the words of this man should be listened to not only because he is the head of the United Nations, the Secretary General, but also because he is a native of one of the countries which we are told lies in the path of Chinese imperialism and which will fall tomorrow if the Americans stop their escalation of the war in Viet Nam. U Thant, as we know, is a Burmese.

July II, 1966
Interim Supply
I think one might be able to make out a case for acquiescing in the perpetration of these atrocities and horrors if we were able to do it in the interest of an overriding moral purpose. This always has been the apologia advanced by those promoting war. It is one I was immunized against half a century ago. I never have been able to detect any solid and enduring gains made by the world from the death and maiming of so many of my generation. It is true enough, of course, that due to the folly and dishonesty of politicians and the greed of those who have a vested interest in a certain form of economic organization, matters are sometimes allowed to reach the stage where military violence is the only course which may be open, when the dragon's teeth sown by folly, dishonesty and greed finally germinate into menacing monsters who must be destroyed if the rest of us are to survive. This in effect is what the United States is telling the world today. They are telling us that the menace of Communism is such that we must not only tolerate but support them in their indiscriminate bombing and burning of the hapless people of Viet Nam. But I suggest it is an abdication of responsibility to take anyone's word for it when we are asked to condone and support actions which fill every decent person with dismay and horror.
Just how good is the claim of the administration in Washington that it is containing Communism? How valid is the claim that Communism would otherwise expand and flow across the face of the earth? In the first place we must realize that when we speak of Communism we are dealing with an abstraction, a very vague and poorly defined abstraction, which conveys very little to us of reality and tells us next to nothing about the men and women who label themselves Communists. This is the crux of our problem with our American neighbours. They see the situation not in political, social or economic terms but in religious terms, and have convinced themselves, and seek to convince us, that what they are fighting is incarnate evil, not flesh and blood men and women. Unfortunately there are those in our own country who have become victims of this type of religious mania.
It is suggested by my hon. friend for Red Deer that the dictates of real politic compel the United States to protect their interests. Again I wonder what interest they have in south-east Asia. They may well have made out a case for their interest in the western hemisphere, but I find it difficult to believe

they can make out a case for legitimate American interest on the other side of the Pacific. In fact, sir, I have reached the conclusion it is not too exaggerated to suggest that United States policies and actions in southeast Asia can be described in clinical terms, if you like, as paranoid. We are dealing with a powerful neighbour who has gone around the bend with religious mania.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
There is a frightening similarity between the tissue of lies, misrepresentations and suppression of facts which have been exposed again and again by reputable United States observers-a stream of misinformation and equivocation which has come from the State Department and from the White House-and the tissue of lies and misrepresentations produced in a shameless rewriting of history which played such a sad part in the history of the Soviet Union. There is a shocking similarity to the more simple and dynamic advocacy of the great lie which was, of course, the policy of the Nazi regime.
A slowly increasing number of United States citizens are becoming aware of this situation and of the symptoms of paranoia with growing alarm. It does seem to me that we in Canada really have a responsibility which goes beyond giving the qualified support our government gives to United States actions in South Viet Nam and which carries us to the point where we should speak bluntly and plainly to our friends and to support the growing numbers of those who feel that this policy can lead only to disaster for the world.
We have heard a lot today and for many months now about Chinese expansion. Curiously enough, we are never presented with any evidence to support that suggestion.
What about Tibet?

I will speak about Tibet. Do you know anything about the McMahon border that was imposed there by the British when they took over Tibet? This was regarded as only a temporary line. China did not storm into India but moved to make a correction there. This was the position taken by the Chiang Kai-shek government before the Communist revolution. This was purely a Chinese nationalist position. Rightly or wrongly, they regarded this section of Tibet as a legitimate part of the Chinese nation.

I had the pleasure not long ago, thanks to the courtesy of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, of having a long interview with one of the senior officials of his department who had recently returned from Viet Nam. I was able to ask him some questions and he gave me some very frank answers. I told him that I did not know whether he could answer one question, or that anybody could answer it, but I asked him if he would give me the benefit of his opinion. I said that we are told repeatedly that the bulk of the people of South Viet Nam support the Saigon government. I asked him what his estimate would be in this regard. He told me that I was right, that he could not give a definitive answer and that nobody else could. He said that his impression was that perhaps 10 per cent' of the population supports the Viet Nam Saigon government, that 10 per cent support the Viet Cong and that the other 80 per cent wished to God that we would get to hell out of there and leave them alone. I suspected that was the position of the people of Viet Nam. I cannot imagine that they are very worked up by ideological preferences. People who have suffered 25 years of war are not likely to be worried too much about ideological niceties.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Peterborough because he displayed what to me is a shocking ignorance of the history of southeast Asia. Apparently he has forgotten the 25 years of history since the French tried to reimpose rule on what was then known as Indochina. No one at that time ever questioned for a moment that the French were faced with anything but a domestic insurgence. True enough, it was led by the Communists, perhaps because no one else would lead them or no one else was capable of doing so. The French were finally forced into defeat at Dien Bien Phu.
Then we come to some more interesting rewriting of history which leads people to speak today in this chamber as though there were either legitimately or factually two Vietnamese nations. A reading of the history of the past 25 years shows quite clearly that there was a temporary demarcation drawn along the 17th parallel which was not to be deemed as a permanent international boundary. A part of the Geneva agreement refers to elections to be held in both sections of Viet Nam.
Then we have another piece of rewriting of history. We say: Oh, well, the South Vietnamese are not bound by any agreement
Interim Supply
because they did not sign it. Of course they did not; neither they nor the North Vietnamese had any authority to sign that agreement because at that time France was the recognized power. France signed the agreement on behalf of those people and they are bound by it just as much as the French were when they signed it.
As I say, I have not yet been able to read or hear of any single incident of Chinese expansion. It may be coming, I do not know, but there has been no example given of it as yet and there has been no example presented to the International Control Commission of the United Nations of any infiltration of Chinese troops. In fact, I think it was just this morning that a report on the radio stated that the Chinese had decided they were not going to involve themselves in the Vietnamese struggle by sending troops there. I think we have to clear our minds of these things and really deal with some facts.
To me the most dreadful feature of this whole situation is that we are now embittering relations between the Asiatic people and those of Caucasian origin probably beyond repair for a generation. I cannot think that the people of Asia are going to feel able to trust the members of our race for a very long time to come. We are told of the aims and aspirations of the United States and how it seeks to develop the country under its control or under its-I think one can only use these words-puppet government in Saigon. How very curious are the things which happen in that country. Some of you may have read the story the other day of wounded Vietnamese children who require plastic surgery. You may have perhaps read that the British were prepared to take them and treat them free in the Mclndoe institution at East Grinstead in Sussex. Other similar offers came from Switzerland and other parts of Europe. The only problem involved was the problem of transportation. The United States had transports travelling to Europe and were asked whether they would provide the transportation. President Johnson flatly refused to do so.
When I was in Europe about three or four weeks ago I came upon another incident of the carelessness and callousness of most of the world to the victims of this war. An organization has been set up to look after Vietnamese children who are orphans and whose parents have disappeared, including some who are wounded and ill. It may be interesting to those of you who shudder at

the word "Communism" to know that only-one country agreed to take sick Vietnamese children, those who are tubercular and have other diseases. That country is Yugoslavia. Other countries were prepared to accept surgical cases but they were not prepared to run the risk of taking children who may have Asiatic diseases. Yugoslavia was prepared to take them and has now taken some.

Our main question is, of course, as the hon. member for Peterborough suggested: What should Canada's policy be? I think there can be no question whatever, after the evidence of the results of our Prime Minister's plea, that our quiet diplomacy has failed and if we are to affect affairs in southeast Asia we must seek some other method. I think sometimes we underestimate the influence and prestige of Canada in the world. I think we underestimate our prestige in the eyes even of our neighbours in the United States. I can think of nothing that would more quickly cause the American president to at least look again at his policies than if the government of Canada were to align itself with now the majority of the other nations of the world in demanding that the United States take another look at its policies and seek some way out of this appalling impasse in which they find themselves.
To return to my hon. friend for Red Deer, I would suggest that anyone who is prepared in the interest of realpolitik to ignore the sufferings of the Vietnamese, both South and North, who have been suffering this sort of thing for 25 years and now have it intensified, surely has a very strange scale of Christian values. I may be considered perhaps as impractical, but I still think that any nation that is prepared to condone this sort of thing will eventually suffer for it, and I suggest we are suffering for it today in the eyes of the world and in the eyes of ourselves, because most of us know that our self-respect has been seriously impaired by the attitude of our government in pursuing this now fruitless policy of quiet diplomacy that affects no one, does not affect events and has merely resulted in getting a kick in the teeth which every Canadian should resent.
The Prime Minister of this country does not belong to my party, but as a Canadian I bitterly resent the fact that the American President should so ignore his advice as to almost immediately, after the advice was given that the Canadian government viewed with some misgiving any escalation of the war, escalate it. How much more savagely do

we want to be kicked in the teeth-because apparently we are kickable people who just come back and ask for more. I suggest that we stop asking for more and join the other peoples of the world in trying to drive some sense into those who devise the policies of the most powerful nation in the world, about which policies so many of their own people have so many doubts today, and among these people some of the really important intellectual and political figures of the United States are to be included.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise not to participate in the debate on the subject under discussion but to ask the government house leader if he would clarify the situation. The government is asking for four months interim supply which would give them supply until the end of October. On the other hand, in today's Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day there is a motion in the name of the Minister of Public Works that this house, when it adjourns, shall stand adjourned until Tuesday, September 6. If this is so, it has a bearing on what opposition there will be to granting the supply sought. If this is a firm date to which the house will recess, I think it is unnecessary that the government have four months supply. I think three months supply would be sufficient. Would the government house leader be prepared at this point, because it will have a bearing on the debate from now until we pass interim supply, to tell us what the position is?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I should explain, Mr. Chairman. As hon. members know, the rules of the house provide that a motion for adjournment, other than to adjourn until the next day, requires two days' notice in writing on the order paper, and a notice for extending hours of sitting requires two days' notice. Otherwise there is a right of veto in the house and any individual member who refuses unanimous consent can prevent either of those subjects being dealt with. Consequently, a week ago I placed on the order paper a notice of motion for extended sittings with a view to having it available when the house was ready to bring this part of the session to a conclusion, but we did not proceed with the motion. When it became clear that the days I had mentioned in the notice of motion had gone by I had to draft another and give notice today of another motion for extended hours of sitting.
With regard to the date for our return after the summer recess, it is our wish to do this
July 11, 1966



by agreement. We were unable to reach agreement as to the date of our return, so I put a notice of motion on the order paper reading as follows:
That, when this house adjourns at the end of the sitting of the day on which this motion is adopted, it stands adjourned until Tuesday, September 6-
The reason for the choice of Tuesday, September 6 was that this date had been mentioned at the time we assumed the house was adjourning for the summer recess, on June 30. That was the reason for that date. Agreement was not reached among the representatives of the other parties. It was an arbitrary date put into the notice of motion so that notice would appear on the order paper, and when the subject matter did come up it could be dealt with and whatever date was satisfactory could be put in. We have already gone 11 days past the anticipated date of adjournment and we have no agreement yet as to what the date of adjournment will be.
We have two other difficulties. The reason for asking for four months interim supply was that we had intended to have the house come back on September 6, deal with second reading of the Bank Act only and refer it to committee, with the hope that the committee would meet during the following three weeks and the house could adjourn in order to permit the International Labour Organization and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, both of which organizations are meeting in September, to have some use of the House of Commons at that time.
I think it would meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen if we chose another date. I still do not know when we may expect to adjourn this part of the session, but I would think that a more realistic date for reconvening is the first Monday in October, namely, October 3, rather than September 6.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We would be prepared to conduct discussions with the leaders of the other parties on that basis right now. If we do not reach a satisfactory agreement on the point I will be asking to amend the motion when it comes before the house.

Mr. Chairman, I would hope, as the minister is in such a conciliatory mood, that he would agree to a period of three months for supply. Whether we adjourn to September 6 or October 3, three months supply would cover the situation. If we re-

turned on October 3 we would have seven or eight days in which to discuss interim supply.
I would hope, therefore, that the four months for interim supply could be reduced to three. Furthermore, although I am not one to whom the government gives information in advance-

speechtext:
Oh, you do pretty well.

-there have been strong rumours from well-authenticated sources that on the basis of the obvious disagreement that has taken place respecting the wage negotiations with the employees of Canadian National Railways, the disagreement being of such an extent that all three members of the commission have different views, it might very well be that the house would be called back in August should it become necessary to do so. That being so, I would ask the minister to reduce the period from four to three months. After all, interim supply for four months is rather unusual. If we come back on October 3 we will still have lots of time within which the government could bring before the house a motion for interim supply for another month. In that way we would come to a consensus now. If, as a result of a failure of negotiations with the Canadian National Railways employees, parliament might be called together by the government in order to assure the continuance of railway operations, there would be no harm done by reducing the period.
Let me say again that the calling together of Parliament on the railway question is not my suggestion but a rumour that has emanated from sources which have an unusual capacity of prophesying the future actions of the government. I am sure that the minister, with the most desirable purpose in mind of bringing about agreement, would not see any difficulty in reducing the four months period to three. Furthermore there is no disagreement on our part as to the alteration by amendment of the date for the recall of this house as suggested by the minister.

Leader of the Opposition mentioned that the house might have to be called back in August to deal with the labour dispute. I am not prepared to agree with that proposition. That was not my proposition; it is just a rumour concerning the government's intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not prepared to rely on that rumour. If it does happen, I am quite sure that the purpose of calling back the house in August would be to meet that emergency. The house would wish its time to be available to deal with that emergency situation and not with interim supply.
The situation with regard to supply is much better at this point in the session than it has been for a good number of years. About ten departments have been dealt with in committee of supply and the final appropriation bill was passed. The study of the estimates of some eight other departments has been completed by the standing committees to which the estimates were referred this year for the first time. This is in addition to the estimates of the ten departments which have already been passed by the committee of supply.
Four other departments have been before the committee of supply, two of which have been dealt with by the committee for a short period of time. Five other departments are now before standing committees and in the process of being considered. As a matter of fact the consideration of these departments by the standing committees is almost completed. One department is being held over for a supply motion debate which will take place when necessary in the latter part of the year.
In view of the advanced stage of work on estimates I hope the right hon. gentleman will reconsider the request for four months supply. Bearing in mind also the priority we must give to the banking legislation on our return, I hope he would agree to four months supply. The supply debate could then take place in the middle of October which I think is a realistic way of approaching the business of the house. I must say this is a subject to which I have given a great deal of attention in the last two or three weeks. It seems to me this is the best way of dealing with this matter in view of all the circumstances.

speechtext: I wish to say a few words regarding the proposal made by the house leader a moment ago that this parliament reconvene on September 6.

speechtext: You mean October 3.

speechtext:
The original proposal was to reconvene for the purpose of considering the Bank Act and then to adjourn so as to vacate

the chamber for certain activities that are to take place here. I must say that this proposal would amount to limiting the time of debate on the Bank Act. May I ask the minister whether the revised version of the amendment is not to call the house back in September

suggestion I made originally because my understanding at that time was that the house would be recalled on September 6 to make the Bank Act available for study in committee, and then adjourn. Mr. Chairman, up to now the discussion on the supply motion has been on Viet Nam. I have no intention of speaking on Viet Nam. However, Mr. Chairman, you might wish to discover whether there are other speakers on Viet Nam or whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs might wish to answer some of the comments that have been made on Viet Nam before I proceed with this other subject.

Mr. Chairman, in view of recent occurrences affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I feel that I should take the time of the committee for, I hope, not too long to express my views on those occurrences since this is the only opportunity I will have before the summer recess. I do so because in my opinion what has happened in

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
the C.B.C. recently is a sorry story, one that does no credit to the corporation. It requires airing before it is too late to correct the situation which is now developing in the most important single corporation, in my opinion, in Canada.
For what we are faced with at the present time, Mr. Chairman, is the resignation of 11 people as a result of this most recent development. They include Reeves Haggan, supervisor of public affairs, Douglas Leiterman, Patrick Watson, Robert Hoyt, Ken Lefolli, James Carney, Gabriel Michaelides, Beryl Fox, Larry Zolf, Stephen Patrick and David Ruskin, many of whom are recognized as being some of the most talented producers and writers with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We have also had the burial of the program "This Hour Has Seven Days", which while by no means a perfect program was without doubt the most important and most popular program produced by the corporation.
Because these events are the immediate result of what has recently happened in the C.B.C. I feel impelled to make some statements with regard to the situation. I am confident that what has happened has shocked the Canadian people. I am also confident that what has happened is an indication of such mismanagement by the corporation in its most delicate area of work that members of parliament must be concerned about the matter.
I entirely agree, Mr. Chairman, with the statement of the Secretary of State and of the broadcasting committee and with many other statements in many other places that the government ought not to interfere with the running of the C.B.C., and that parliament should not interfere with the day to day operation of the corporation. But I suggest to you that if there is a case, as in my view there is now a case, of utter mismanagement of an important situation, which I shall try to document in the few minutes I will take, then it is for parliament to discuss the matter and if necessary to take some steps in connection therewith.
I want to make clear first-I do not think I need to do so but I want to do so for the record-that I, like most members of this house, have, if you like, the most passionate feelings of support for the role of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and for the contribution that that great institution

has made to the cultural and artistic development of this country, as well as its contribution to the dissemination of information and to public discussion and debate.
I also want to make clear that despite the various things I had to say in the broadcasting committee about the "Seven Days" programs which I happened to see, and I saw many of them, I did not necessarily subscribe then, nor do I necessarily subscribe now, to every segment of the program every week I saw it. There were some parts of the program which I thought were in poor taste. There were other parts of the program which other hon. ladies and gentlemen might have thought in poor taste. But that is irrelevant to the essential fact that the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" was, first, a most popular program which attracted over three million viewers, twice as many as any other program in the history not only of the corporation but of any other Canadian program.
Second, the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" had a great many aspects of imaginative, adventurous and useful presentation of fact, opinion and controversy in this country.
Third, I do not defend, nor do I feel I have to defend, all of the actions of Mr. Leiterman and his associates since their difficulties first arose. Indeed, I do not hesitate to say that despite my great admiration for Mr. Leiterman and most of his associates it is my opinion that some of the things which they said and some of the steps which they took were ill-considered and might not have been said or taken. That again is irrelevant to the basic issues. Those who, both in the press and in this committee, attempt to get away from the basic issues, which I think are clearly there, by saying that the producers acted wrongly here or acted wrongly there seem to me to be doing a disservice to the C.B.C. and to the major aspect of and the reason for the existence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, about which I shall say a few words, mainly in the language used by the white paper which was tabled by the Secretary of State.

In fact, I have always been highly impressed by the intelligence and dedication of the president, Mr. J. Alphonse Ouimet, whom I have had
