the pleasure of knowing for a good many years. I do not for a moment deny the very important contribution he has made to the development of the C.B.C. in many directions.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, and these are the points of importance and relevance to the present unhappy and sordid situation in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I suggest to this committee that the evidence is absolutely clear that there was in the first instance, when Watson and LaPierre were removed from "Seven Days", admitted mismanagement, and insensitiveness in the way in which they were removed. And in what has happened in the last few days there was on the part of top management of the C.B.C., and I choose my words carefully, nothing less than vindictive, reckless behaviour, with the result that irreparable harm has been done to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, particularly to the important and delicate public affairs department, in the loss of important talent to the corporation and in the resulting widespread loss of morale throughout the creative and production personnel of the corporation. This is why there have been wholesale resignations.
I said that in the first place there was gross mismanagement in the Watson and LaPierre matter. The evidence before the broadcasting committee of parliament clearly and fully justifies my statement. There was gross mismanagement in four directions, every one of which is fully supported by the evidence which any member can read in the proceedings of the broadcasting committee.
As we were told by the president and by vice president Walker when they gave evidence for top management, the problem of "Seven Days" had been with the corporation for two years. Anybody on the broadcasting committee who had had any experience with organization found it impossible, I am sure, to understand how management of the corporation could let things slide for two years, if there were problems, without doing anything decisive about those problems.
Second, and more important, Mr. Chairman, there was an admitted breach of necessary procedures. This was admitted during the evidence before the committee and is indicated in the report of the broadcasting committee, which pointed out that there had been for more than one year an unwritten understanding between top management and the producers that no member of a production team would be fired, turfed out in any 23033-474
Interim Supply
way, without consultation with the producers or executive producers. Captain Briggs admitted to Mr. Keate that that was so, as Mr. Keate points out in his report, and Mr. Ouimet admitted in evidence before the broadcasting committee, as did Mr. Walker, that there was this breach of necessary procedure in the corporation and that top management entirely ignored the breach and refused to do anything about it.
This was not a formal matter. The line of communication which had been created between top management and the producers was not merely a formal procedure that had to be gone through step by step. It was seen, as one reads Mr. Keate's report and as one reads the report of the broadcasting committee, that a need for communication existed, and that it was of the essence of the possibility of creative people doing their job at all. Indeed, there was not merely an understanding between the producers' association and the corporation. The contracts for executive producers which were filed with the broadcasting committee made clear that such contracts contained the provision that the executive producer or the producer, as the case may be, had the responsibility for the selection of scripts and principal artists.
The line of communication to which I have alluded was not merely an understanding but was actually a requirement of the contract with, in this case Douglas Leiterman. Yet what happened? Mr. H. G. Walker himself, without speaking to Mr. Leiterman, without assuring himself that Mr. Leiterman had been consulted-this is in the evidence- jumped over Mr. Leiterman, spoke directly to Mr. Watson and told him that his contract with "Seven Days" would not again be renewed. Everyone who has dealt with this matter, and particularly Mr. Keate, has expressed regret that this breakdown in communications took place.
Without taking time to read any section of Mr. Keate's report, may I say that any hon. member can satisfy himself that he expressed regret that this had happened, as also does our committee's report.
Third, Mr. Chairman, and this perhaps is the serious part of the mismanagement of the whole affair, if management was dissatisfied with "Seven Days", if management felt that something had to be done about the content of "Seven Days", then obviously it had to discipline, if it was going to discipline anyone, those responsible for the content of "Seven Days", namely, the producers. What

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
did management do? Instead of doing anything about Mr. Leiterman or Mr. Hoyt or Mr. Lefolli or the director or anyone of those responsible for the content of "Seven Days", it fired the two hosts. Yet the evidence before the broadcasting committee was clear that every word Patrick Watson and Laurier LaPierre spoke as hosts was scripted for them. They did not write a single word. They did not say a word that was not written for them. When they were conducting their interviews, in every case they were pre-taped and were later edited by the producers. Again, those two men had no responsibility for what appeared on the screen.
When these facts were pointed out to Mr. Ouimet and to Mr. Walker, they gave different reasons for firing LaPierre and Watson. They said it was not as a result of any attempt to improve "Seven Days" at all; it was because they felt that LaPierre was not a good interviewer, because he wore his feelings on his sleeve and conducted interviews to the detriment of the person interviewed. So far as Watson was concerned, they wanted to separate him from Leiterman and that was why Watson was fired. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that never in my lifetime have I heard so weak and indefensible a defence of an action that could not otherwise be explained. If anyone was to be disciplined for "Seven Days" it should not have been Watson and LaPierre. The management which did what it did is clearly guilty of extreme imcompe-tence.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I will return to that in a moment, but I turn now to my fourth point concerning the most astonishing piece of mismanagement of all. The evidence is clear that when it was suggested to Mr. William Hogg, the director of news and public affairs, and to Mr. Hag-gan, the supervisor of public affairs, that something should be done about Watson and LaPierre they said in effect,-I am paraphrasing, but it is all in the evidence and I am paraphrasing accurately-"let us not do it now; let us wait until the season is finished or almost finished, because if we do it now it will interrupt the work, it will do harm to the program, it will create a fuss; let us wait four or five weeks until we are near the end of the season." It should be clear to a schoolboy that if top management had had the elementary common sense to wait until the season was almost over, say until May 7 or 8 instead of April 6, and then had said that in the fall the program would begin again with

whatever personnel they chose, all the fuss and bother which has occurred would never have occurred.
Surely it did not require a genius to see that the request of Mr. Hogg and Mr. Haggan that the matter be left alone for a few weeks was reasonable and sensible. But not Mr. Walker. Whether or not Mr. Ouimet or Captain Briggs were responsible for Mr. Walker acting like a bull in a china shop, as he did again the other day, I do not know. But I do know that any management which times its action so badly, which takes action against the two people who were identified in the public mind with the program but who were innocent in regard to the results of the program about which management was being critical, any management which does that shows an incompetence, indeed, a recklessness of which this parliament must take note.
It also seems clear to me as a citizen who has never had occasion except in friendship to deal with men and women of creative talent-I have had the pleasure of knowing many of them-
And dealing with them professionally.
Yes, I have dealt with them professionally, as counsel for ACTRA in particular.
Ah, ah. That is interesting.
The hon. member says that as though he did not know it. I made it clear to the broadcasting committee and I make no apologies for it either.
I just said it was interesting.

I am glad something I say is interesting to someone. As I say, I have known many of them and dealt with them, but I have never had occasion to direct or supervise or have that kind of association with them. But I do know it is obviously impossible to deal with creative people in an organization like the CBC, as it was suggested though not proven before the broadcasting committee that a management person had declared, the same way as you run a canning factory. The reason for the requirement of constant communication between producers and top management is not merely for formal purposes but because it is impossible to get the best out of creative people, whether they
July 11. 1966



be reporters for a newspaper or producers for a broadcasting corporation, if they are treated as mere units, if their ideas are not carefully considered and if they are not carefully consulted about their program and their work.
The objection, therefore, to Mr. Walker jumping over the shoulders of the producers to go after Watson and LaPierre in the way he did is not merely an objection, as Mr. Walker and Mr. Ouimet tried to make out, because certain formal procedure had been abridged. It is based on the fact that an important part of the work was ignored and an important way in which to make the work effective was entirely disregarded.
Everybody agreed that the "Seven Days" program should continue. Mr. Ouimet told the committee on many occasions that he wanted it to continue, but improved, cleansed, if you like. Mr. Walker emphasized that he wanted "Seven Days" to continue. Mr. Keate in his report said by implication that "Seven Days" is an important program and should not be lost. The broadcasting committee report says by implication, as I read it, that such programs as "Seven Days" ought to be on the screen this fall by asking the corporation to make sure that adventurous public affairs programming will be carried on this fall.
Indeed, the C.B.C. board of directors itself in a statement issued on May 27, 1966, which is an appendix to No. 18 of the committee's proceedings, says, as found on page 1098, that the board supported management's position with regard to Watson and LaPierre out of a deep concern for the maintenance of C.B.C. policies and to continue with the program "Seven Days".
Everybody wanted "Seven Days" to continue. But what was the result? The result is that "Seven Days" is now dead. It will not continue. And I cannot escape the suspicion that when Mr. Ouimet and Mr. Walker told us and when Mr. Ouimet told Mr. Keate, as Mr. Keate says in his report, that they wanted "Seven Days" to continue, they were talking with tongue in cheek and had no intention of letting the program continue this fall. They were playing a game with the parliamentary committee and with Mr. Keate and were being less than honest both with Mr. Keate and with us. This is a shameful thing, I suggest, for important executives of an organization like the C.B.C. to do.
May I also point out that everybody concerned agrees that Leiterman and Watson are brilliant producers. The board of directors of 23033-4741

the C.B.C. in the same statement at page 1097 says:
In management's view, both Mr. Leiterman and Mr. Watson are very able and highly talented.
But these very able and highly talented men have now been forced out of the corporation. One was, in effect, fired and the other was forced to resign. The directors go on to say as found on the same page:
"Seven Days" was largely their creation and together they gave it a character and thrust which were to some extent at variance with C.B.C. policy. This was intended at one time to be called "Quarterly Report". Whether or not it will appear in view of recent events is a different story.

Mr. Keate, at page 19 of his report, quotes President Ouimet of the C.B.C. as saying when asked, "Why did you fire Watson and LaPierre-why not Haggan and Leiterman":
We recognize that Leiterman is a brilliant producer an we believed in the show. We felt that it could be improved. When we took a firm line, the show improved and its ratings climbed steadily upwards.
This is the man, speaking to Mr. Keate as he spoke to the broadcasting committee, who is responsible for getting rid of Leiterman and forcing the resignations of Watson, and Beryl Fox who produced the show in which he said he believed.
It is the same with regard to Mr. Haggan, and I think it is important to put these things on the record. At page 17 of his report Mr. Keate, a publisher of a newspaper and a man whose writings suggest he has a highly subtle mind, says:
The C.B.C. Toronto public affairs supervisors, Hugh Gauntlett and Reeves Haggan, impressed me as highly intelligent and dedicated corporation people who felt it their duty to express their disagreement with C.B.C. policies which led to the non-renewal of Watson and LaPierre.

I think if I finish my notes it will take 15 minutes. If that interferes with someone else I can return to the subject later.
I want to deal very briefly with the problem of broken communications related to the present mess that occurred only in the last few days. Instead of taking time to quote I shall simply refer hon. members to pages 10 and 23 of Mr. Keate's report. I also ask them to look at page 1096 of volume 18 of the broadcasting committee minutes and the statement of the C.B.C. board of directors. I also invite hon. members to look at the proposal which management agreed to with regard to communication. From all these they will find that without exception everyone, including the members of the broadcasting committee, underlined the fact that there had been a breakdown of communication between top management and the producers. This fact was underlined not only by Haggan, Leiter-man and Watson of the English speaking network but also by Thibault and his associates in the French speaking network. Yet what happened very recently, Mr. Chairman?
I am informed, and I am certain this is the case, that the Toronto public affairs department presented top management of the C.B.C with a memorandum containing a proposal to end the difficulties and to come to some understanding that would promote the work of the public affairs department. I am not interested whether they were right in their proposal or not, but I understand that in it the Toronto public affairs department, with the understanding or consent of the Montreal public affairs department, made concessions to management.

For example, they agreed that LaPierre should not come back as a host. They agreed that Watson be taken off the editorial board and any other agency connected with "Seven Days" which had anything to do with policy, the execution of policy and the programming of "Seven Days". They made other concessions of that sort. It does not matter whether their proposal was good or bad. I am not here to judge that. What matters is that right up until this moment Mr. Ouimet and his associates have not found it necessary to hold any discussions on this proposal with Mr. Haggan, Mr. Gauntlett, Mr. Thibault or anyone else representing the public affairs department.
Despite the admission of Mr. Ouimet that communications had broken down, despite the statement of Mr. Keate, and despite the statement of the broadcasting committee, Mr. Ouimet and his associates, Mr. Walker and Captain Briggs, continue to ignore the breakdown in communications. Even when given an opportunity to hold discussions with the people concerned to see whether or not they could arrive at some kind of solution that would retain this talent for the corporation and for the program "Seven Days," and thus improve the general morale, the breakdown in communications persists.
As is indicated in various reports, and particularly in an article by Christopher Young in last Saturday's Ottawa Citizen, Mr. Leiterman was first given until five o'clock on Friday to decide whether he would accept a proposal to renew his contract under certain conditions and, if not, whether he would head up a new "Document" series which the corporation would let him produce, but suddenly the Friday five o'clock deadline was brought forward to four o'clock on Thursday. Further, when he was given a new condition for his contract, as Mr. Young points out, and asked management whether he could have 24 hours to discuss it, management said no.
Again, all the requirements of communication were broken, undoubtedly because Mr. Ouimet and his associates, not the board of directors, it seems to me, but the top management on Bronson avenue, had decided Leiterman had to go, that "Seven Days" had to go, and they did not care what the consequences were in terms of the loss of talent to the C.B.C.
I should like to quote from the article by Christopher Young in last Saturday's Citizen:
It seems transparently clear that this elaborate trickery was designed to get rid of Leiterman without actually firing him. It was typical of head office methods throughout the dispute. Regardless of
July 11, 1966

what one may think of the "Seven Days" program or of its producers, these methods surely demonstrate to the public and to the government why the C.B.C.'s management is not trusted or respected by its working staff.
The result of all this can be summarized in the following, and I rush to my summary so as not to take more time than I said I would. First, the C.B.C. lost, and it may be that Canada will have lost, a group of talented people. No doubt there are other talented people on the staff of the C.B.C., and I have no doubt other talented people will develop and come to the C.B.C. No person, no group of people is indispensable to the C.B.C. or to any other organization, but in the meantime this group of highly talented people is lost to the C.B.C.
To what purpose? What has the corporation gained? I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman-again I choose my words carefully, even though they are strong-nothing except obviously the vindictive satisfaction of some members of top management in hitting back at those they probably hold responsible for causing them some discomfort in the last few weeks.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
The second result of all this terrible behavior of top management is that the most important and most popular program of the corporation, "Seven Days", is lost. It is not to be improved as Mr. Haggan said it should be improved. At page 498, No. 8 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, Mr. Walker quoted Mr. Haggan from a memorandum prepared by the latter and presented to top management as to the ways in which he would like to improve the program "Seven Days" and Mr. Walker ended by saying he could not have said it better than Mr. Haggan put it in his memorandum. Yet Mr. Haggan will not be there to improve it, Mr. Leiterman will not be there to produce it, and the program will not be there. What will we have in its place? Some bland, unexciting and probably quite unuseful, if I may use a word less offensive than "useless", program such as some hon. members may have seen last night in place of "Compass".
As have other hon. members, Mr. Chairman, I have followed with interest the work and development of the C.B.C. I have observed it now for at least 35 years and I believe one of the major contributions of the C.B.C. always has been in the development of greater unity in Canada through the dialogue
Interim Supply
between English and French speaking Canadians. One of the major parts of this contribution was a program to be developed in 1967, our centennial year, and to be called "Quarterly Report". It was to have been a bilingual and bicultural program. Whose idea was it? According to the evidence before the committee it was the idea of Mr. Haggan and Mr. Thibault, Mr. Pat Watson and some French network producers. How was it to be produced? It was to be produced by the group which produced "Seven Days" and the group that produces "Le Sel de la Semaine" on the French network. But Mr. Haggan and Mr. Watson are gone; the "Seven Days" group is gone. I venture to say that the program "Quarterly Report" is gone despite the fact that it was to be not only one of the major contributions to the dialogue between English and French speaking Canadians but, as it were, a merging between English and French speaking parts of the country. This is but one result of the insane, vindictive behavior of the management of the C.B.C. in the last few days.
The ills of the corporation to which I refer are recognized not only by the members of the broadcasting committee. These ills of the C.B.C. were recognized, indicated and described by the Glassco commission report, by the Fowler committee report and, most important of all, by the president's own study group headed by Mr. M. A. Harrison who gave evidence before the broadcasting committee. I suggest that by implication the white paper of the Secretary of State and the government also criticizes these ills in the C.B.C. All of these things were before top management, the Glassco commission report, the Fowler committee report and the report of the president's study group, as well as the parliamentary committee report and the white paper. All these things were ignored by Mr. Ouimet, Mr. Walker and their associates.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the Secretary of State that while I agree entirely that neither parliament nor the government should interfere with the internal administration and day to day operation of the corporation, the management of the corporation is a government responsibility. The persons who head the corporation are appointed by the government. It does not matter whether it is the present government or a previous government. The government has responsibility for those who are appointed to

manage the corporation. I suggest that neither the Secretary of State nor the government nor the members of this committee can ignore the irreparable damage which has been done to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by those who have been entrusted with making it work and making it work for the benefit of Canadian people.
Unless steps are taken now to redress the wrong which has been done to the people of Canada by the loss of this roster of important talent to the C.B.C., and unless steps are taken now to get rid of the top management of the C.B.C. and their recriminations in dealing with the creative and production people of the corporation, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will become, as my leader the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested the other day, a corporation with a great number of executive people and no talent. That is the dangerous position in which the whole behavior of top management of the C.B.C. has placed the corporation.
I think it is time we ended all these illnesses in the C.B.C., the failure of communication between top management and the producers, the lack of confidence from the top to the producers and from the producers to the top, and the unhappy situation at the middle management level. All of these illnesses in the C.B.C. have been pointed out for years now, but the intelligent, durable head of the corporation, the president of the C.B.C., Mr. Ouimet, goes on ignoring these reports and remains durable to the detriment of the corporation and to the detriment of the development of Canadian talent and Canadian creativeness.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Certainly.
Does the hon. member think he has helped

Does the hon. member think he has helped find a solution for the benefit of all Canadians by what he has just said?

I think so. I think the Secretary of State and the government ought to take steps in respect of the president of the C.B.C.,

who is an appointee of this parliament and this government, and when I say "this government" I do not mean the one in power at the moment but the government of Canada. In my submission, Mr. Ouimet should be spoken to by the government and told, not asked any more because he has ignored suggestions, that the situation in the C.B.C. must be reviewed and that the talent which the C.B.C. has lost must be gained back in order that the purposes of the corporation for the benefit of the Canadian people may be fulfilled.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to deplore a situation which has developed in the conduct of the affairs of the C.B.C., as the hon. member who preceded me deplored a situation. I deplore it from the opposite side of the chamber and indeed perhaps the opposite side of the Canadian national political spectrum from that on which he stands. I deplore the situation of rebellion and threat of anarchy that has crept into C.B.C. operations in the past few weeks arising out of one of the most colossal displays of petulance and temperament that it ever has been our misfortune as television viewers, newspaper readers and broadcasting listeners to experience in our lifetime.
I do not for one moment defend the action of management in the events leading up to the "Seven Days" chaos. I do not defend this action of management because, although management has the unquestionable right to manage, as all of us have insisted from time to time, it does not have the right to botch and mismanage; and this is what happened in the "Seven Days" situation. Furthermore, I have little sympathy for a management that got itself into trouble by placing in positions of authority over creative people narrowminded bureaucrats who have no comprehension whatsoever of the creative mind, the creative spirit and the creative temperment.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
But having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would also say that I have no patience either with creative people who deliberately set themselves upon the path of obstructionism and rebellion for the sake of obstructionism and rebellion. And this is what happened in respect of the latest situation regarding the C.B.C. public affairs and "Seven Days" crisis.
The hon. member for York South has talked about creative people whom he has known. I have known some creative people too, and I dare say that everyone in this
July 11. 1966

chamber has known and worked with creative people in their jobs outside this chamber either prior to or since coming here. The creative spirit is a spirit that all of us admire and desire in this country. It is probably the single indispensable spirit in the world. The artist certainly makes us what we are. But there is a difference between a mature artist and an immature artist.
The producers of the C.B.C. "Seven Days" unit and other producers from the public affairs area have enjoyed considerable public sympathy in the past few weeks, both at the outset of their dispute and subsequent to the height of the "Seven Days" crisis. They enjoyed a sympathy which was generated in their behalf because of the C.B.C. management's aptitude for ineptitude in the business of managing a broadcasting operation. But I have no hesitation in suggesting that such individuals as Messrs. Leiterman and Watson, Miss Beryl Fox, and the rest in that group of eight or nine, dissipated all the good will they had acquired, by their petulant, precipitous outbursts of last week when they all resigned.
Someone has said that the difference between an immature man and a mature man is that an immature man wants to die for a cause while a mature man wants to live for one. This proverb best expresses, in my view, the thing that is wrong with the temperamental rebels of C.B.C. public affairs who are pouting on the sidelines voluntarily this week.
The problems of the C.B.C. are problems that go a great deal deeper than those that revealed themselves in the "Seven Days" crisis. As the Secretary of State said, the "Seven Days" situation was just the tip of an iceberg. The iceberg, I suggest, is far more serious than many Canadians imagine. The biggest thing wrong in the C.B.C., in my view, is that irresponsible producers have been allowed their heads too long by a management that is either blind or hamstrung by politics.
The hon. member for York South said that Messrs. Watson, Leiterman, et al are brilliant producers, and he quoted many references which used that term. I think I need hardly remind the erudite member for York South that brilliance is no excuse or justification for immaturity and irresponsibility. At the least these producers have only been guilty of irresponsibility and immaturity. At the worst they have been guilty of the insidious spread of destructive propaganda.

They do not run perhaps as far to the left of the spectrum as those of the hon. member for York South, but certainly they run substantially to the left of the position that I and several other members of the broadcasting committee hold. The hon. member quoted from the Ottawa Citizen and Mr. Christopher Young so perhaps I can be permitted the indulgence of the committee to quote from an oracle which I think in this context is considerably more authoritative. I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press.
Oh, oh.

She is doubtless aware that the Winnipeg Fress Press and I do not always see eye to eye, although we both stand for Winnipeg and what can be good and great about Winnipeg. I suggest, however, that in this context the Winnipeg Free Press is a substantially reliable authority precisely because its political philosophy is inclined to the left of that philosophy to which I and some of my colleagues on the broadcasting committee adhere. I refer to the stand we took in respect of management's rights in this situation.
The same position as Christopher Young took.

The hon. member for York South suggests that it is the same position as that which Christopher Young took. I doubt if the positions are precisely the same, but I will accept the hon. member's remarks because I think he will find this editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press of July 5 instructive and provocative. The editorial under the heading "C.B.C. News" reads as follows:
Recently, at the centre of a bitter C.B.C. dispute, the question of editorializing by the corporation's hired hands became an issue. That is, as distinct from the hands the corporation is bound to hire to do some editorializing in their own behalf, as professional commentators.
How long must we wait before the C.B.C. restores its new broadcasts to news reporting and leaves the comment to the outsiders it invites to take the air?
In reporting on the difficulties faced by Mr. Wilson with respect to his support of U.S. policy in Viet Nam, Mr. Michael Maclear in London but formerly of the Far East, betrays the gift of sight and

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
dwells on the inner intentions of the Red Chinese. According to the stand taken by the CJ3.C. executives, the C.B.C. and its staff have no such insights and ought not to have. The job of a reporter, even a C.B.C. reporter, is to report.
Mr. James M. Minifie from Washington, puts more editorial opinion into his tone of voice than any other C.B.C. reporter, but he excelled himself as the filterer of meaning when he reported that the National Council of Churches in the U.S.A. "representing 41 million members" of its constituent churches, had called upon ministers to protest the Hanoi bombings.
The National Council of Churches does not in fact "represent" anything. It is an ecclesiastical body that exists for certain practical purposes in the areas of consultation and co-operation. Its opinions mean no more than that they are the opinions of the people who expressed them. Yet the import given by Mr. Minifie to their resolution was that 41 million American churchmen had joined the hue and cry against the bombing of oil depots and other military targets in North Viet Nam. The impression spread abroad in Canada, that the American people are increasingly hostile to the U.S. commitment in Viet Nam and to the way it is being carried out, is due in considerable part to people like Mr. Minifie of the C.B.C. and to the slanted choice of Canadian and American commentators who seem to represent almost constant hostility to the U.S. position in Asia.
The C.B.C. was once a reliable and unbiased reporter. That cannot any longer be said of it and it is time the matter got the attention of whatever vice presidents have any mind left for their jobs.
The hon. member for York South will now perhaps appreciate the implication of my suggestion that this is a provocative report considered in the context of that journalistic oracle from which it came. I doubt that even Mr. Young of the Ottawa Citizen has ever taken that honest, conscientious, introspective and objective a view of the malaise-if I may borrow that term again from the report of the broadcasting committee; and I refer to the true malaise-that affects the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and through it the moral fibre and fabric of this country.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I suggest that over the past few years a cant has been allowed to develop in C.B.C. public expressions and articulations that is damaging and dangerous to this country, and the very reputation of the C.B.C. is at stake. I cite once again the editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press to which I have just referred. I have heard quite frequent references in discussions with journalists whom I know, and with some of whom I have worked in the past, on this particular subject of C.B.C. news, news reputation and news integrity. There is no question in the minds of some of them that the manner in which C.B.C. public affairs programming, programs like "Seven

Days" and certain interviews have been conducted has been damaging and detrimental not only to C.B.C. news but to the news profession in general.
I do not think anyone in this chamber can deny that in certain instances public affairs interviews on C.B.C., particularly on "Seven Days", have been little more than exercises in verbal assault and battery and bludgeoning of the interviewed subject. In consequence, a number of young reporters-and I have spoken to some of them of tender years-men and women of conscience, who were trying to learn their trade, have come to the conclusion that this is the way interviews should be conducted-that this is the way one goes about getting the facts of a story. Anyone who has had any passing acquaintance at all with the profession of journalism knows that this is arrant nonsense and, worse, it is destructive nonsense.
I think the very integrity of C.B.C. news is at stake in this issue. I know there are certain legitimate newsmen in the C.B.C. who are very concerned with the deleterious effect that C.B.C. public affairs programming in the interview field has had on their work and professional reputations in this country and the United States.
The reputation of the C.B.C. as an international broadcasting operation, and more than that, as a news-gathering operation, was once one of the highest to which anyone could aspire in that field in the world. I do not think anyone would deny that in our lifetimes the C.B.C. developed a reputation and a name beyond reproach in the field of public affairs, news interviews, general broadcasting operations and the general field of story coverage. I suggest that this reputation, this stature, is now facing considerable threat and is in danger as a consequence of some of the techniques which have been allowed to develop, which have been allowed to come to fruition by weak management or hamstrung management in the C.B.C., and which have been expressed and articulated through this production group which was at the root and core of the "Seven Days" crisis this spring.
So what there is wrong with the C.B.C. basically, in my view, is a loose rein in management's hand. I suggest that the country will be better, that the reputation of the C.B.C. will be better, that the news fraternity and the journalistic and broadcasting professions in general in this country will be better, and everyone will be happier, if the eight producers who resigned last week from the
July 11, 1966

C.B.C. are allowed to remain resigned, and il the C.B.C. gets on with the job by delegating production responsibility for those disputed programs to other production centres and units in Winnipeg, Halifax and Vancouver if need be.
I think the opportunity is at hand to strike at the heart and the root of the C.B.C. problem, and if we attempt to exercise it now the C.B.C. will be restored within a very short period of time to the stature and level of estimation it has always enjoyed. I suggest that this is the course that members of this house and the broadcasting committee in general should take in the weeks ahead. The browbeating, the petulant rebellion, the immaturity has gone far enough. At this point, although I have attempted in my services on the broadcasting committee to remain objective-and I do not think I am the only member of that committee or the house making this confession-as far as the C.B.C. producers of the "Seven Days" unit are concerned, I say goodbye and good riddance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will of necessity be very brief. I am rather surprised, as a matter of fact, that so late in the session we should be discussing, in a period of time as important as interim supply, the problems that' have confronted C.B.C. not only for the last few months but, as the previous speaker mentioned, for the last couple of years. I would have thought that in view of the report brought down by the broadcasting committee, in view of the Keate report, in view of the White Paper and in view of the report tabled by C.B.C. management, we would have exhausted the subject of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in general and "This Hour has Seven Days" in particular.
Reference was made earlier to the political leanings of the hon. member for York South as opposed to the political leanings of the hon. member for Winnipeg South, and I wonder just where I stand when I say-and I hope someone does not say "on the fence" -that I agree with both hon. gentlemen in their appraisal of what has happened in the C.B.C. First of all, very early in the committee meetings-and there were 22 or 23 of them-I expressed the opinion, in examination I believe of the president, Mr. Ouimet, that I was rather surprised that management had waited so long to manage. I expressed the opinion and the dismay that Mr. Ouimet had
2303.3-475
Interim Supply
waited so long to rectify what must have been for management an intolerable situation.
I think it was obvious to all of us who sat on that particular committee that management was incapable of managing. I think this was well documented in the 22 or 23 sessions we had and in the reports that have now been printed and are public knowledge. When I heard the president of C.B.C., or some of his vice presidents, talk about up the line and down the line, it brought back pleasant memories of the days I worked with Canadian National Railways, and it seemed to me that somewhere between top management and the producers the up the line and down the line ceased to function; in fact, there seemed to be a strong case that could be made for derailment.
In this respect I share the opinion of the hon. member for York South in his criticism of management, and I very strongly share the opinion of the hon. member who has just finished speaking, that these young, articulate, brilliant producers took full advantage of the chaos that existed within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I expressed the doubt early in the committee meetings, as a result of my questioning of Mr. Watson, that "This Hour has Seven Days" could properly be considered as falling under the department of public affairs.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
As I said, the success of "This Hour Has Seven Days" is that it succeeded in arriving at a formula which was partly news, partly entertainment, partly sensationalism and a great deal of bias. The bias has worried me ever since I first became an ardent fan of this program. I have expressed on several occasions sympathy toward the abolitionists' cause in the recent debate on the death penalty, and I thought this program showed a definite bias toward abolition which was unfair to those viewers who were entitled to exposure to the other side of the question,- and indeed there was another side to it.
I felt a little concerned about the definite bias shown in the Viet Nam problem. Although I consider myself fortunate to have had the opportunity as a member of parliament to be exposed to both sides of this problem, I often wondered what happened to the hundreds of thousand of viewers who looked on "This Hour Has Seven Days" as gospel truth and who were unable, not necessarily because of lack of education but because of lack of opportunity, to be made aware of the fact that there were two sides to

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
most controversies that "This Hour Has Seven Days" exposed from Sunday to Sunday.
Despite its imperfections and its bias, I was a great fan of this program and feel it should remain on the C.B.C. I think, Mr. Chairman, that it was well explained, well documented and well established; that this program, vital, interesting and exciting as it was, was going through a period of trial and error and that modifications would have to be made if the program were to continue. I feel these modifications would have to be outlined, introduced, implemented and enforced by management and nobody else. The guidelines for this type of program should not be outlined by the producers but should fall within the general policy of the C.B.C.
The C.B.C. is an organization of which all Canadians should be proud. I think in the main it is a wonderful example of responsible televising and responsible radio broadcasting. Programs such as "This Hour Has Seven Days" have a definite place in Canadian television, but I share the opinion of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg South, that management must manage. The C.B.C. management has demonstrated its inability, ever since this program has come on the air, to control these articulate, eloquent and, if you wish to call them so, creative young producers who have had control of "This Hour Has Seven Days".
There is a malaise in the C.B.C. So far two speakers have emphasized the background of this problem. I share the opinion expressed by the hon. member for York South that the C.B.C. management is inept and should be straightened out and that steps should be taken-and indeed this is the government's responsibility-to see that the C.B.C. is properly administered. This can be done without violating the written rule of the House of Commons that we should in no way interfere with the internal management or dictate the policies of the C.B.C.
However, I think, Mr. Chairman, that the producers have had their day in court and that they realized the good will they had generated not only in the committee but among the public. Had they realized they had exposed the general malaise in the C.B.C., which was broader than that which affected their own program, and had they been satisfied to leave it there, chances are that this program could have been produced in the fall and that the majority of men on that program would have taken part in it.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that the report which was recently tabled was slightly biased, not in the remarks it included but in those it excluded. I do not intend to get into a debate on that subject except to say that on one occasion some remarks which I thought should have been included and which would have created a little more balance in the report were unfortunately removed, quite legally, at the next meeting which, unfortunately, I was unable to attend. Events since that time have proven my point and I do not intend to belabour it.
I might say, in concluding my remarks, that I feel very sorry about the departure of Reeves Haggan. This man was a stranger to me when he first appeared before the committee, and he is still a stranger to me. I had never met him before and I have never met him since, but he struck me as a man dedicated to his job. He sided with his producers, he had the courage of his convictions and he resented top management's interference in this program. He was hampered by a lack of direction from a very wishy-washy board of directors and general manager. I do not think either C.B.C. or Canada can afford to lose the services of Reeves Haggan.
His plans for a program known as "Quarterly Report" which was to appear this coming season are badly needed as we approach confederation. It was to be a joint program that would have, perhaps for the first time, managed to show all Canadians that the cultures of the two founding races complement each other. This program would have been different, one in which the English Canadians would have been proud to participate and which the French Canadians would have enjoyed, because it would have shown them the best of another culture with which many people are unfamiliar. Should this particular type of program be a victim of this trouble and malaise within the C.B.C.? I am sorry if this is so, and I would appeal to the minister and to the present management of the C.B.C. that even if "This Hour Has Seven Days" does die, as certain pessimist's feel it will-though I am not of that opinion,-then every effort should be made to produce the program "Quarterly Report".
I consider that one of the weaknesses of the C.B.C., despite its size, its almost unlimited funds, its freedom and structure, is that it has not been a strong and dominant force of unity in this country. It has not been either a
July 11, 1966

force of unity or disunity: It has been neutral. Reeves Haggan and Mr. Thibault realized this fact and secured a mandate from management to do something about it.
That was one of the few bright periods in the 22 or 23 meetings we held with the C.B.C. management and producers. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South I should like to say I hope this chapter in Canadian broadcasting history will not be repeated. I sense the Canadian people are fed up with the subject. Indeed I and most hon. members in the house are tired of it. I am surprised this subject has come up because I do not think it is urgent and I do not even think it is any longer important.

Mr. Chairman, I should also
like to refer to the interim supply we are being asked to vote today, but I want to deal with a few different matters which also come under the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh).
There is a problem
If the hon. member for Lapointe wishes to speak on another subject, I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether I might be allowed to speak prior to his remarks?

speechtext: Would the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) yield the floor to the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) who has wanted to deal with the subject under discussion since early this afternoon?

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to allowing the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke to speak on the same subject, but I do not want this to become a precedent, because if I let everybody speak for three days on end about the C.B.C., when my turn comes, I shall have no opportunity at all to deal with matters which might interest me on interim supply. Since the member for Okanagan-Revelstoke is anxious to speak about the C.B.C., I do not mind yielding the floor to him for the time being, but I hope that afterwards you will allow me to proceed with my remarks.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with considerable interest to the comments which have been made about the 23033-4751
Interim Supply
C.B.C. I too would question the raising of this topic at all at this time. I was one member of the broadcasting committee who questioned even the wisdom of rushing as we did to issue a report, when it seemed to me that we had already served the function that was asked of us, so far as the "Seven Days" controversy was concerned, of being a sounding board and a place to air the opinions of both sides on the particular matter.
The haste with which the report was assembled had something to do with this lack of balance to which reference has already been made in debate. It is also incidentally one more objection to the holding of committee meetings while the house is in session, because the fluctuations in the attendance of members on that committee as it drew up its final report were great, and the report as finally presented to the house was not the sort of report it might have been had the entire committee sat throughout its preparation.
I was interested indeed to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South, and I congratulate him for providing in this afternoon's sitting a balance to the political spectrum that for far too long during the committee sittings was missing in the questioning of witnesses before the committee. Better late than never; and I think the hon. member in his remarks this afternoon has gone a long way toward correcting the balance.
In the opening remarks of the hon. member for York South I think we heard perhaps an unparallelled example of a plea for power to be handed out without control. This was the factor that was crucial to the entire discussion before the committee on the subject of "Seven Days", namely who was actually in charge, and what was the nature of the power that lies in modern communications, particularly in television?
I think a situation has been growing where the people who are actually working in the medium, the producers, have realized that they have been given power, and that the top management of the C.B.C., which has failed in the past to realize the power they have been handing out to the producers, has come only gradually to a realization of the immense amount of power it has distributed to the producers to shape Canadian public opinion.
In spite of all the professions of the hon. member for York South that he was striving for complete accuracy, a measure of the accuracy of his remarks can be found by

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
observing his use of the word "fired" over and over again in his remarks. I think without exception that every time he used that word, it was not quite the fact in the particular case about which he was speaking.
I do not intend to air at any great length the pros and cons of the program or of the dispute. I too enjoyed the program on most occasions when I saw it. I was however very concerned on several occasions about the direction that it was taking and about the dangers of what seemed to me to be a lack of control somewhere along the line, whether by middle management or top management. The program did not always seem to be under control.
I mention this because I was the first member to raise in this house the question of the hour-long documentary on the drug "L.S.D.", which eventually resulted in a statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and some concern being expressed by the government over the dangers of this particular drug and its use among young Canadians. This to me was the best example of a program that lacked balance, in a situation where it is questionable whether even balance would be desirable in a program of that nature. Even after it was programmed on the English network the French network made further contributions along the same line which did nothing to solve the problem created by this drug in Canada. In fact, it probably aggravated the situation.
Always with public broadcasting we have the paradox that the taxpayers are asked to contribute to something of which they might not approve, which is a most delicate situation to be in. I do not accept the argument that creative talent can never be restrained, that somehow it must be allowed to run with absolute freedom. It seems to me that control is essential, particularly in public broadcasting. If the creative talent object to the very slight control that is placed upon them, then they have the opportunity to try elsewhere. But as long as they work with a public broadcasting corporation they are, in a sense, obligated to follow the lines that have been laid down for them.
The hon. member for York South referred to the long, long time during which the situation was allowed to develop. He found it a strange example and thought it might be the result of mismanagement. It seems to me that if anything the C.B.C. was too lenient, as evidenced by its lack of control over this particular program.

I have no brief at all for the measures that they ultimately took to bring the program into line. I think that they have acted foolishly, and on occasion weakly, in attempting to do something about the situation. But if the public is to be asked to finance broadcasting, at considerable public expense then we must have people in the corporation who can exercise some control, and we must expect them to exercise that control in the interest of the public.
I doubt whether any good would be done now by attempting to bring the program back. It is said that one never bathes in the same stream twice, and I think it would be an exercise in frustration to attempt another year to revive the program "This Hour Has Seven Days". We may be saddened by the fact that it has gone. However, if the government now acts with dispatch and insists that the C.B.C., not parliament, members of parliament or the broadcasting committee, has control over programming and if it exercises that control to produce programs of the sort that the Canadian public would expect, then I think that perhaps some good has come from the controversy.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak about a matter also under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State and I shall conclude my remarks with a statement of our views on the current dispute within the C.B.C.
I should like, today, to bring up a question of primary concern for the civic authorities of the city of Quebec. It is the matter of a detailed model of the Old City of Quebec which was made, carved and designed between the years 1806 and 1811 by a gifted engineer Mr. Jean-Baptiste DuBerger, including all the fortifications of the Citadel of Quebec, the very fortifications designed for the military defence of Canada when the Americans tried to invade the country in
July 11, 1966

1812. As I was saying, this model was prepared by Mr. Jean-Baptiste DuBerger, including all the fortifications of the Citadel of Quebec, the very fortifications designed for the military defence of Canada when the Americans tried to invade the country in 1812. As I was saying, this model was prepared by Mr. Jean-Baptiste DuBerger on the orders of Col. By, who is well known in Ottawa and who, in fact, is the engineer who built the Rideau Canal.
It so happens that this model is now in the Museum in Ottawa; it is owned by the federal government and it is on view' in the Museum in Ottawa. But the authorities of the city of Quebec would like the federal government to show this model of Old Quebec produced by Jean-Baptiste DuBerger in the city of Quebec itself; this would be helpful in many ways: from the historical viewpoint, from the tourist viewpoint and it would also be helpful to the engineers, the architects and the town planners of the city of Quebec for the urban renewal operations of Old Quebec. The engineers would be most interested in having it to renovate one of the oldest cities on the North American continent, the city of Quebec. On that question, the mayor of Quebec, Mr. Gilles Lamontagne, wrote to the Prime Minister on March 1, 1966 the following letter:
Mr. Prime Minister
Some years ago, the municipal council of the city of Quebec officially asked to have returned the celebrated DuBerger model.
You are undoubtedly aware of the value of this work and it would be logical for your government to agree to its return to the city of Quebec where it would be most useful not only from a tourist viewpoint but also for the renovation operations of Old Quebec. Furthermore, should your government agree, it would be more logical to return this model to the city of Quebec rather than to the government of the province of Quebec, as suggested to us by the Historical Monuments Commission in a letter, copy of which is attached.
I trust, Mr. Prime Minister, that this matter will receive your immediate attention.
Please accept my highest regards.
Gilles Lamontagne Mayor of Quebec
On March 11, 1966, the Prime Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Mayor,
I duly received your letter of March 1 informing me that Quebec City is interested in obtaining the "DuBerger" model.
I asked my colleague, the minister responsible for the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada, to take your request into consideration and to inform you directly of her decision.
Yours sincerely,
Lester B. Pearson
Interim Supply
That was on March 11, 1966. Six weeks later, that is, on April 29, the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) replied to the letter of March 1 as follows:
Mr. Mayor,
I regret not having replied earlier to your letter of March 1 to the Prime Minister, in which you ask for the return of the famous model of Quebec City, built from 1806 to 1811 by captain John By (later promoted to the rank of colonel), of the Royal Corps of Engineers, and by Mr. DuBerger, military surveyor and member of the garrison.
By the way, I wish to point out that in the Secretary of State's letter, there is a mistake which was corrected and which I shall correct myself later on, with the help of some notes provided by the Chamber of Commerce of Quebec City. The minister goes on to say in her letter:
In order to clear up the misunderstanding which seems to persist regarding this model, it might be a good idea to explain that it has never belonged to Quebec City or to Lower Canada. Up to 1910, it belonged to the British Department of Defence which first needed it to draw up defence plans for Quebec City against a possible attack by the United States. That is why it was sent to Great Britain when completed in 1811. In 1910, it was brought back to Canada as a gift of the British government to the Canadian government for all the Canadian people. You realize that it would be quite improper for the Canadian government to part with a gift received under such conditions.
I might add that without the help of this model, the Natural History Branch of the National Museum of Canada would be unable to do justice either to the history of your province and Quebec City or to the history of national defence in our country.
I am fully aware of your interest in this model and I realize that it would prove useful in effecting restoration work in Old Quebec. I shall be glad to send you pictures of the model, some of which are very good. It goes without saying that your architects can come to Ottawa to examine the model which is on view in the Daly building.
Yours truly-
This letter is signed: Judy LaMarsh, Secretary of State, minister responsible for the model.
It is safe to assume that the recipients were far from pleased with this letter and that several points could be taken up in the minister's reply. That is why, hardly seven or eight days later, or on May 6, 1966, the mayor of Quebec City, Mr. Gilles Lamontagne replied to the Secretary of State as follows: My Dear Minister,
I am in receipt this very day of your letter dated last April 29, in answer to the letter I wrote to the right hon. Prime Minister requesting the return to Quebec of the famous DuBerger model.
I have noted your summary report of the history of the preparation and peregrinations of this work which, according to you, "would make it absolutely unconceivable" for the government of Canada to

July 11. 1966
Interim Supply
relinquish a gift received from the British government "for the whole of the Canadian people".
With much respect, I take the liberty of differing in opinion as to what you consider an absolute impropriety; the population of Quebec City is still Canadian, as far as I know.
II I may digress, I wish to say that the minister must have been flabbergasted by that answer, when she received this letter. I read on:
I really wonder why "without the help of that model, the Natural History Branch of the National Museum of Canada could not do justice either to the history of our province and of the City of Quebec, nor to the history of this country's national defence", if that model were to be exhibited in the City of Quebec, the oldest and most historic city in Canada.
That an outright grant of the model to the City of Quebec seems improper to you, is conceivable to me. But, I really do not see any serious reason which would prevent the government of which you are a member from exhibiting the model on premises located in Quebec City, under the control of the Natural History Branch of the National Museum of Canada.
Are the Battlefields Park, the Citadel, the harbour facilities and the post office, to cite only a few examples, not federal property, belonging to the whole of the Canadian people, although they are located in the City of Quebec? I sincerely believe that as much can be said about the historical works found there.
The Grande Hermine, which the federal government recently decided to rebuild for anchorage in the limits of Quebec City after Expo '67 will remain the property of the Canadian people. I sincerely believe that the Canadian government has given proof of its wisdom in deciding to exhibit it in Quebec City; in that sense, the government of which you are a member has understood that that historical reconstruction "belonged" to Quebec.
In the same sense, I believe that the DuBerger model "belongs" to Quebec City. If only for the sake of exhibition to our own public, in the city of which it represents a section very dear to us, it would be, in my humble opinion, a sufficient reason for the return of that model from Ottawa to Quebec City.
But we have more serious reasons. Indeed, when, in co-operation with the provincial Department of Cultural Affairs and the members of certain intermediary bodies, we are starting the development of a program for the restoration of Old Quebec, it is obvious that this model would be extremely useful to those who have undertaken to carry out rapidly this restoration which is necessary not only for us, Quebeckers, but for all the Canadian people. We consider that Old Quebec occupies the first place in our national heritage.
For that purpose, only the model's photographs which you offer to us would naturally not suffice. Moreover, the possibility for our architects to come to Ottawa for consultation according to your suggestion, cannot be considered as convenient. The great distance between Quebec and Ottawa would make the consultation costly and certainly less frequent, hence less effective.
Finally, for the centennial of the confederation, it is important that the model be exhibited in
[Mr. Gregoire.l
Quebec City, true centre of that national constitution.
After that account, I hope that you will reconsider your decision and that you will recommend the "return" of the DuBerger model. I am sure such a transfer can be brought about without disrespect toward historical proprieties; it would even improve on present conditions.
Yours truly,
Gilles Lamontagne Mayor of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to add a few remarks made by the Chamber of Commerce in that connection. After reading all the exchange of correspondence, the Chamber of Commerce thought it proper to make a few remarks in its official organ Realisons.
In answer to an argument advanced by the Secretary of State, we can read this:
Even though the Quebec model was carried out under the orders of Major By, he is not the designer and even less the sculptor. As a matter of fact, Major By has taken no part at all in the creation and the making of the model even though, until 1831, the work was attributed to him by error. The controversy over the origin of the Quebec model has lasted long enough during the last century that it is useless to raise it once again in 1966, when in 1831, a copper plate was affixed to it, attributing it to DuBerger only. The idea was to pay a post mortem tribute to the inspired engineer who died in 1821.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
The Chamber of Commerce adds:
We do not ask the Canadian government to give up this precious relic, but rather to give it a place of honour in historic Quebec to which it belongs.
Further, it says:
It must not be forgotten either that during two centuries the destiny of the country was directed from the Chateau St-Louis. The orders of the Duke of Kent, father of Queen Victoria, and those of a good twenty French or English governors general of Canada were given from the Chateau St-Louis.
Under the circumstances, the right place for the DuBerger model would, again, be the historic ruins of the Chateau St-Louis, at least partially restored. Concerning such an initiative, we appeal to the patriotism-
And I add, for the information of the hon. lady, if she will listen to me-
I am a Canadian patriot.

To continue:
Concerning such an initiative, we appeal to the patriotism, understanding and generosity of the Canadian government.
Finally, placed in historic Quebec under the custody and protection of the federal authorities, that model would constitute not only a lesson in legitimate pride and preservation of historic Quebec for the people of Quebec, but also a splendid
July 11, 1986

history lesson for the thousands of Canadian taxpayers and American tourists who visit us every year.
Respectfully submitted on May 17. 1966.
The Chamber of Commerce of the district of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, in view of the facts, I would like to ask the Secretary of State the following questions: First, since there seems to be a difference of opinion with regard to the history of the model, would the Secretary of State be willing to have a real study made about the history and the peregrinations of the DuBerger model?
Second, would she be ready to reconsider with the members of her department and the director of the National Museum of Canada, the advisability and possibility of repatriating the DuBerger model to Quebec City?
I think that the minister could have that study of the history made and could also ask her senior officials to reconsider that matter.
There is a whole sector of the population who would like to see the DuBerger model transferred to Quebec City for tourist and historical reasons. The municipal council of the city of Quebec would also like to have that model on view in Quebec City, in order to make it easier for the Quebec engineers to restore Old Quebec.
I hope that the Secretary of State will take this request into serious consideration and will see to it that it is complied with. Since I am able to do so, I act as the spokesman in the house for the mayor of Quebec City and the Chamber of Commerce to ask the minister to reconsider the matter. Knowing her great understanding and patriotism, I hope that she will return that model to Quebec City.
Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that, when considering interim supply, we are allowed to talk about all kinds of things, I would also like to take this opportunity to discuss a particular subject, while the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is in his seat. Not so long ago, that is on June 24, 1966, we received from the office of the Minister of Finance, a news release about the Small Businesses Loans Act. It gave statistics about the loans made under the act to small businesses between January and March 31, 1966 and I would now like to quote a few figures.
The small businesses in British Columbia secured in the three-month period covered by the news release from the Minister of Finance
Interim Supply
loans amounting to $846,292 out of a total of $5,091,885.
In Ontario, loans amounting to $2,066,159 were made to small businesses, while in Quebec they amounted to only $760,977, approximately 12 or 13 per cent of $5,091,885. On the other hand, in a small province like Alberta, $497,039 were loaned.
I would ask the Minister of Finance to find out from his department why there should be such disproportion. Why is it that, under the Small Loans Act, three times as much can be loaned to Ontario as to Quebec? Not that I am against Ontario being given $2,066,159 in loans; but I should like to know why so few have been granted in Quebec. Still, we know many requests are made for loans by small businesses in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to know why that federal enactment does not allow for granting as much in loans in the province of Quebec as in Ontario or in British Columbia? Indeed, the latter received $846,292 in loans, while Quebec got only $760,977 in loans. In other words, a small province like British Columbia received 80,000 worth of loans more that a large province like Quebec. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance to look into the matter and tell us why the disproportion is so great.
I notice, for instance, that in 1965 the difference was not as marked: British Columbia received $879,616 and Quebec, $1,467,205, out of a total amount of $5,550,933. That is approximately 25 per cent. It has been diminishing lately. I would ask the Minister of Finance whether we could have an investigation?
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) is not in the house now but I wonder if the minister would convey to him certain remarks I wish to make about his department.
I have here a letter sent by the Department of National Revenue to parishes, to parish priests, to churchwardens, to vestry boards and concerning:
Re: 1966 T4 Information Return.
That letter was sent in English. I have here a letter sent to the cathedral of Hauterive, on the north shore, county of Saguenay.

I would therefore ask the Minister of National Revenue to see that those forms are translated-I know that there are some in French-and distributed. It is not sufficient to have them printed in French. It would be an excellent thing if the officials, who absolutely wish to act as dictators by reducing receipts for charitable donations, should at least write in French in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I am going to deal with another department. I have before me a letter which might amuse a few members of the house; it concerns the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Please note that I have nothing against the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; far from it, I think it does a good job and I gladly praise it when the occasion warrants. I congratulate the authorities for a recent improvement. For some time, I have noticed that the officers on the hill are bilingual and can easily converse with the french-speaking and english-speaking tourists. However, it might sometimes be useful to remind Commissioner MacLellan of certain facts, to keep him on his toes and encourage further improvements, things are looking up, but there is still a lot to be done. It may be the slowest department to get moving, perhaps because the R.C.M.P. is the slowest on the uptake.
I have received a letter from a school teacher, I shall quote a few excerpts. This fellow was driving to school to teach on Tuesday, June 21, 1966 and there is every indication that he was going a bit fast in the Gatineau parkway; he does not say he did, but a R.C.M.P. constable proved he was going a bit too fast. However, according to this letter, the R.C.M.P. officer did not stop the teacher immediately, but only 10 minutes later. He waited for the teacher to reach the school yard, and in full view of about 500 students, as the school bell rang, the R.C.M.P. officer made his entrance with his siren on; to make matters worse, that same fellow, a native of Hull, tracking down speed violators, did not know a single word of French. And this, in the province of Quebec, in Hull, at the Saint-Jean-Baptiste high school in Hull. I quote:
At 8.55 a.m., a young constable, W. D. Maxwell got out of his car shouting "What do you think you're doing?", or words to that effect, which sounded to me most arrogant. Hundreds of students were drifting toward my car. I politely asked him to repeat and apologized for not understanding English. Feeling a bit foolish, I imagine, and in spite of the students' jeers, he had the nerve to ask two of them to act as interpreters.
July 11, 1966

And I can very well see Hull high school students acting as interpreters for the Royal Canadian Mounted police.
And the teacher goes on:
I tell you all this as a protest against the uni-lingualism of the R.C.M.P. constables in Quebec territory, against the arrogance of the colonial greenhorn who stopped me, against the disturbance this officer created in a school, where even in ordinary circumstances, it is not easy to impart good education; he held me up to my own students, as a model of misconduct, and I feel that in so doing he undermined the very foundations of the educational system. If I committed an offence, it was outside the school property.
And that is not all; the same teacher goes on:
And that is not the end of the story. This afternoon I have telephoned the R.C.M.P. headquarters, to demand apologies for their way of enforcing law and order. Witnesses will confirm that I was referred to six officers one after the other, some of them apologized politely, others bawled me out, before I could get a single French word in edgewise. The little French speaking constable to whom I spoke promised he would take my complaints to his superiors (naturally he was in a subordinate position being French Canadian). A little later on, he called me back to let me know that only in court could I demand a review of the situation and a different approach to value.
And he adds:
-the stature of the R.C.M.P. is not enhanced by this business. And Ottawa will wonder why young Quebeckers are separatists . . . and anarchists-
Mr. Chairman, this took place in a Hull school, before 500 students, where the R.C. M.P. agent had to ask students to act as interpreters.
I believe a complaint should be made against such actions. Since the complaints made here against unilingualism of R.C.M.P. officers on the Parliament Hill were profitable, I think the same complaints should be made against this R.C.M.P. agent who was on duty in Hull and who, moreover, thought it proper to go and prove in a school of 500 to 600 students that, being on duty in the province of Quebec, he did not know a word of French.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I hope the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), responsible for the R.C.M.P., will take this remark into consideration in order to urge further the R.C. M.P. commissioner to see to it that this police body which can do a good job in certain fields, can also improve in other fields to give satisfaction.
Mr. Chairman, these then were a few desultory remarks I wished to make. I trust they will be taken into consideration and that a solution will be found fairly soon to the problems I have pointed out.
