speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question?
But of course.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I did not want to interrupt the honourable member, neither while he read his numerous letters nor during his speech; that is why I waited to put this question.
A while ago he spoke of the repatriation of the DuBerger model. Does he mean that that model once was in Quebec City?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, according to the statement of the Chamber of Commerce I read here, it was there once; it was built there by one Jean Baptiste DuBerger between 1806 and 1811. It stayed there, at the seat of Government of Lower Canada at the time. It was only after the end of the war against the Americans that British troops took it to England. Those troops had not fought the war; as you will remember, that war was won at Chateauguay, near Valley-field, by the troops of Colonel Salaberry, a good French Canadian of those days. The model came back to Canada in 1910, and today the citizens of Quebec would like it to come back to Quebec City for tourist and historical reasons, but most of all to facilitate the renovation of Old Quebec which the city of Quebec and the Quebec Department of Cultural Affairs have recently undertaken.
I trust the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), whom I see in the house, will support my request and that of the authorities of the Quebec District Chamber of Commerce, the mayor and municipal council of Quebec so that that old model, now located in Ottawa, can be sent back home within the old walls of the city of Quebec.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, this probably is one of the problems in this type of debate where we keep moving from one subject to another, but I should like to go back to the C.B.C. difficulties. I suppose I could activate Jimmy in that regard; he will understand. I think the problems of the C.B.C. have always been really in the never-never land where the government is not supposed to interfere, and yet parliament is supposed to make the decision as to what the C.B.C. stands for. I do not say this in any policital party sense, but it is interesting to note that in the years that the C.B.C. has been in operation there have been many conservatives in this house. They

July 11. 1966
Interim Supply
appear to be on all sides of the house, on the left, on the right, and in front of me. I am sure that anyone who has been here very long will realize that the right and left wings of parliament do not necessarily stand with the political parties. I think it is true that there are many who say the C.B.C. is safe, for the simple reason that over the years it has been able to establish a status quo; it does not offend anybody and certainly does not step on any toes.
There are also those who would like to see the C.B.C. become a vibrant force, the developer of Canadian nationalism. For this reason I think in this debate there has been a lack of idealism. I think the major problem which faces the Canadian public today is their lack of ability to make any correction, change, or expression of desire in respect of the Canadian broadcasting system. It always has been interesting to me to note that my political party, the New Democratic Party and previously the C.C.F., always considered the C.B.C. to be a holy cow about which you did not say anything bad, and you attacked anyone who was going to say anything about it. When debates were taking place and everybody was congratulating the C.B.C. for the advancements it made in the field of drama, which I did not understand at all, I was interested, in the success achieved by Don Messer's Islanders, as a summer replacement. I am sure its success shocked the C.B.C. officials as much as did the "Seven Days" dispute. They tried to remove the Islanders and found that it was rated about the second highest of all the programs. Finally they had to yield to the demand of a large segment of the public and keep Don Messer on.
I am one of those who believe the C.B.C. has a number of functions. If you can squeeze in drama and probably anything else that is good for people, along with entertainment, this is all to the good; but entertainment should not be disregarded entirely. I am sure the C.B.C. was shocked to find that the program 'Seven Days" was receiving such a wide audience appeal. I never have stood up to talk about "Festival" because I think those who run "Festival" are a bunch of nuts, and that a lot of the programs are like that. This is just a personal opinion. I know nothing about drama. I have not criticized it because I thought it must have some good in it and that perhaps people liked it.
I did like "Seven Days". In the last election when I travelled through my constituency I was surprised to find when I entered a house

when the "Seven Days" program was on-and this followed Bonanza-that you could not talk to the people at that time. I have had an opportunity to watch "Seven Days" and considered it to be a very good program. I feel that if they put on eight or ten items and I am only mad at one of them, they have done pretty well for me. If everyone found the same thing, I think it did very well for them.
It is all well to talk about Minifie. I never saw such a deadpan announcer. He is like an announcer on a local radio station who, when announcing the death of someone, made it sound like a hilarious occasion and when talking about the strike-made it sound like a wonderful thing. I think on "Seven Days" there has been a very good balance. This is something which I think most of those who have resented "Seven Days" appear to forget. The three million persons who watched the program considered it to be a pretty good program. Maybe one person phoned Bud Walker and said it was bad, and he made a public apology. He apologized for a situation at St. Vincent de Paul that did not require an apology. I know this from first hand experience because I was there. I know that it was not as complete as it might have been, but what was taped was a two hour program and it had to be cut down to eight minutes. I agree that the warden did not get as much time as he might have, but he got some time. I participated in this program, did not get any time, and I did not complain to Mr. Walker. I believe his apology was unwarranted.
When I hear these weak sisters stand up in parliament and talk about the grand and glorious picture of parliament which must be given, I say that if you must have this, then get out of politics. We want an interview to be dynamic. I can even get sick when I see Charles Lynch interview the Prime Minister, and carry him for 60 minutes. The Prime Minister of this country has a great deal to give to the public and he does not have to be carried by someone with an opposite view. Everybody knows where Charles Lynch stands politically. I was ashamed of that program. I was ashamed of the fact that there was a need to build a little wall around somebody. If they need that, then they should not be interviewed.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It seems to me that the interviews carried out on the "Seven Days" program were well done, and I think particularly of the interview of Mr. Bundy, conducted by two young
July 11. 1966

men. I went to the C.B.C. offices shortly afterwards and asked Bud Walker how he would like to have conducted that interview. He told me that he would not have wanted particularly to conduct it. A great many complaints were made because Bundy took over the interview from beginning to end, and would hardly allow the interviewers to ask any questions. I give the two young men full credit for the efforts in the interview, because Bundy is such a capable man he could take over the whole show. If it were not for the fact that these young fellows got a little belligerent they probably would not have got a word in edgewise. This interview was more like a paid political broadcast, and Mr. Bundy acted like the man paying for it, not wanting the interviewers to interrupt.
Surely we must all agree that the management situation is bad. We know that the Prime Minister was blackmailed into appointing Mr. Ouimet as president for another seven years, at a time when he intended to appoint him for only one year. I am sure everyone is aware of the fact that Mr. Briggs was appointed by a previous administration to keep Mr. Walker in line, and to set up what one might consider as a ship-shape organization. This sure is a leaky ship, foundering on the rocks. It has been leaking water for a long time. If I were a dictatorial minister I would reappoint Mr. Ouimet to carry on in his capacity. He has not done a damned thing for the C.B.C. for some time, in fact since Mr. Briggs came on the scene. I would get rid of Briggs and Walker because they have not only done little, but everything they have done has been done wrong and at the wrong time. They could not have picked a worse time to fire LaPierre and Watson. Those two gentlemen became identified with the sympathy of three and a half million viewers.
The French Canadians suggest that LaPierre does not portray the French Canadian, but for my part I think he portrays a very nice type of French Canada, and I like that kind. LaPierre is emotional, gets involved, flies off the handle and cries when it is necessary. Even though the French Canadian people tell you they are not emotional, LaPierre portrays the emotional French Canadian. I do not like separatists, or young people who go around dragging things through the mud and making everything as difficult as possible. I think most English speaking Canadians like and enjoy the type of French Canadian that LaPierre portrayed.
Interim Supply
They believe that the balance created between the emotional LaPierre on one side and the cool and calculating critical Watson on the other was sort of a cultural balance. Whether one agrees or disagrees with my feelings, approximately three and a half million viewers felt that these co-hosts created a cultural Canadian balance. You might think that this was an Alice in Wonderland type of program but I think it was good.
I attended the meetings of the broadcasting committee, not because I had to but because I was interested, and I know many of my colleagues were interested in this situation. Many people in this country are going to ask us, as members of parliament, to indicate which side of this controversy we support. I for one cannot understand how the management side can be justified. If people charged with managing cannot manage, then they are not management. This fact brings to mind a situation which occurred in respect of the Hollinger mine. An individual had 5,000 people working for him. The supervisor told him that he could not find a job for one individual and therefore he would have to be fired. The manager, in reply, suggested that if the supervisor and himself could not find a job for everyone they were not managing the company properly. The management of the Hollinger mine was certainly not benevolent in their approach to employees but they adopted the attitude that there must be a place for everybody, and if a place could not be found management was not doing its job.
Some may think that management has a right to be dictatorial but I do not believe that is true. After all, this is not the eighteenth century. We do have a masters and servants act; but I remember listening to a well known Ontario lawyer argue a case, and I am sure he lost it when it became apparent that he was basing his argument on the provisions of this act. Management has a role and that role is to manage. Employees also have a role, and that role is to give as much service and ability as possible. It is not their position to try to usurp management's role. They must, of course, give the best that they can within the established framework. Surely this is an obligation.
I listened to Reeves Haggan last night on Doug Fisher's show over C.T.V. I think Doug Fisher has an uncanny ability to bring out what is in people. If it is bad, he brings it out; if it is good, he brings it out. He

July 11, 1966
Interim Supply
does not compete or put himself in a competitive position with the person being interviewed. I think he made it obvious that Reeves Haggan is a capable and sincere person and that he left his position because he felt the dismissal of certain producers was not done on a normal and proper management relationship. He was informed that Leiterman was to be dismissed with only two days notice.
This afternoon we were informed how the dismissal of these producers came about. I wonder whether people watching the program last night, after listening to Mr. Haggan, would feel that he was one of a group of young ambitious men. In my opinion he represents the progressive element of the C.B.C., and a young man who is interested in doing his job. At no time did he suggest that he was interested in taking over the C.B.C. At no time was he vindictive.
The situation has to be changed and I suggest the first step to be taken is to dismiss Walker. His dismissal must be arranged. He is the man who is responsible, not only for starting this conflagration but also for pouring fuel on it when it got going. Fuel was provided for this fire also by members of the broadcasting committee, as well as by Mr. Keate and Mr. Fowler.
Who allowed Mr. Walker to go to Toronto in October and take over the operations there? Is the minister aware of the fact that Mr. Walker said he was not going to do this when he was in Ottawa, but that he received a phone call from Mr. Ouimet telling him that he was about to release a statement and that it was to be attributed to Mr. Walker? I have heard a lot of talk about political pressures in the C.B.C. organization, but I do not think there are any as we know them. I believe the situation is much like an insurance company headed by a "Mother Ouimet", who decided that politics had to be involved. [DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Let us take a more cogent example. Let us look at any major union in Canada-and I have had something to do with several of them. There are politics in these unions. They do not call the politicians Liberals, Conservatives, N.D.P. or anything else; but these are politics whereby people are trying to better themselves and set up their own political regime, in the sense of the organization to which they belong. I am rather inclined to believe that the C.B.C. in its lines of demarcation have spent more time on the politics of
(Mr. Peters.]
those lines than on politics as we know them, whereby politicians in the House of Commons have any influence on them.
I doubt whether there are very many people in parliament today who would say we should get rid of the C.B.C. I am of the opinion, however, that there are many who would say, "Don't let the C.B.C. get any stronger than it is. Don't let it have any greater influence than it has. In fact, any problem the C.B.C. has is all to the good, because it may go away by itself.". I think a number of members of parliament would agree that private television might do a better job if the C.B.C. was out of the way. Mr. Haggan was asked yesterday whether he could produce a good public affairs program without money, and he said, "Absolutely not". He was asked whether this was the reason "Seven Days" had been so successful and indicated that it had a reasonably modest budget for that type of production.
The minister just made a comment which I did not hear. I do not know whether she agrees with what I said or not. But the budget varies anywhere from about $12,000 a week to $50,000 a week; so that in discussing it we were never sure how much the budget was. Perhaps when I was not there the committee was able to ascertain exactly the total cost of this program including technical assistance, studio and all the other things necessary. His point was that C.T.V. was providing enough money in some of the productions they were undertaking to be able to produce, reasonably, a better type of television program than they were producing. The reason they were not producing a better type of program was that the people in the C.B.C., built up through the C.B.C. and by the C.B.C., were more capable than any others in Canada. I think this is true and would agree that the producers of "Seven Days" were probably of the top calibre.
I was surprised at the remark a Conservative made in the committee. In view of where he sits I would have thought his position would have been different. Mr. Haggan was referring to Leiterman and called him a near-genius. I do not know whether I would go that far. I do not know what a near-genius is; nor do I know what a distant one would be. I do not even know what mediocre producers are like; this is not my field. But it is my opinion that with a viewing audience of three and a half million the program "Seven Days" was the kind of thing that should have been extended into
July 11, 1966

other fields. I honestly believe that over the years the C.B.C. has developed a very impartial news media that probably cannot be duplicated anywhere. I think its public affairs programs were never of that calibre, and with "Seven Days" we had a program that had a large audience and was presenting things that were controversial and interesting. One hon. member mentioned L.S.D. I watched that program. Some members should pay some attention to these programs and not talk about things they have not seen. I came to the conclusion that I just didn't have guts enough to try L.S.D.
I am quite sure this was brought home to many young people of this country as well. The program did not only show the fantasies produced through taking L.S.D., and the medical aspects of it, but it showed the dangers of taking this drug.
It didn't show enough.

It showed enough that I would not go out and undertake one of those experiments with a sugar cube that somebody gave me on the street. That is the good feature of programs such as this; many people see them and realize the dangers involved in this kind of thing. This is what makes television such an important media. It provided me and a great many other people with information on a subject I did not know anything about, and it provided that information in such a way that I felt I would not have the nerve to take that trip into insanity-
You wouldn't get back.

-or whatever they call it, because I just did not have the nerve. Some members may not have thought of it in that way. Some may have decided they were going to take it. More power to them. I do not want to duplicate anybody's action in this regard. I believe the public is smarter than those members of parliament who are ultraconservative and want to go back in time, rather than forward. I believe the public is smarter than they give them credit for. The public have a right to make a decision on some things, and I believe they are better equipped so do so because of television and other news media. In addition, Mr. Chairman, we have in this country more people with university education than ever before. This applies also to people with high school or public school education. They read, write and can observe and, in my opinion, are well
Interim Supply
equipped to make a decision. Even at election time they make their decision, whether rightly or wrongly. They are now in a position to make that decision. I believe their decision is getting "righter" as time goes by.
In my opinion people are now making better decisions, and I believe that television is a medium that assists them to do this. It is a medium where the individual viewer is in close and immediate contact with the screen and the people on it. I think it provides a much clearer picture of the situation than we would otherwise have.
We know what the press has said about this program. I am surprised at the strength of their opposition to "Seven Days". I would not know whether it was because Leiterman had been previously in the journalistic field; I would not know whether it is caused by petty jealousy; I do not know whether it is the up-staging these people have received. I am not really sure of the reason but have been surprised by it, because I have found that newspaper people as a rule are not resentful of others making an impression on the public, but have enjoyed the added prestige the journalistic type of communication was creating, whether it be in the magazine, television or newspaper field.
I have been surprised at the resentment the press has shown to the desire of young people to make an impression in the C.B.C. organization and obtain some rapport with management and others, to obtain a dialogue to be carried on between top management and the production level so that top management would be aware of what they were trying to do, wanted to do and were capable of doing. Then management would make the decision whether Canada was ready for this type of thing.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I believe that parliament has now to make a decision. Do we go back to the mediocre coverage we were receiving in public affairs programming, or do we continue to expand in this field and go into programs like "Quarterly". The French Canadians will scream blue murder, I am sure, at some of the things that have been said on "Quarterly" because there are English and French speaking people who do not really have an understanding of the program, and the intention of trying to bring the two races together to develop something that will eventually become Canadian talent and Canadian national culture.

July 11. 1966
Interim Supply
I believe this is a role of the C.B.C. and it is the type of role that should be developed. I believe it cannot be developed by the Walkers, by the Ouimets, or by the Briggs. It can possibly be developed by people like Haggan, Thibault, and some of the others who are dedicated entirely to their work, and the people with whom they work.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I think they are willing to experiment, they
are willing to allow for an exchange of ideas in a completely new field. This will not be possible if there is a lack of understanding between the producers of both networks at that particular level. I am assured by some that this can also extend into other parts of th C.B.C., not only in the field of public affairs programming but in other fields. It will be difficult for the minister to sit idly by and not do something about the many reports that have been brought to her attention over the past year or so. If this happens, then the three and a half million Canadians who have watched and enjoyed this program will ask themselves: Why have the members of parliament not done something about this matter? It is not' our duty to interfere in the business of the C.B.C. by firing the individuals concerned or by reappointing Leiterman and re-establishing "Seven Days", but to establish a rapport which will allow for a dialogue and a free exchange of ideas between management and producers.
I believe there should be something for the right and something for the left', and I hope there will be a program in the fall for three
and a half million people to enjoy.

I rise to participate in this debate on interim supply because of the very serious situation which exists in the southern portion of the riding of Bruce, which I represent. This situation exists not only in part of Bruce county but also in the lower part of Gray and the surrounding counties. I am further prompted to speak this evening on the subject, Mr. Chairman, because of the lack of satisfactory answers to questions I have raised in the house in the last few days regarding a letter to the Prime Minister which alludes to a certain campaign promise made on November 4 concerning area development. This promise was made to the people of the Kincardine area.
The subject on which I wish to speak, Mr. Chairman, is the problem which is created when one area has been designated as a

depressed or slow growth area, and the area adjacent to it is not so designated. The communities in the south of Grey and Bruce counties are very much at a disadvantage when they must compete with the other part of the county to attract industrial development and expansion.
We are well aware, Mr. Chairman, that under the existing legislation these sectors do not qualify for designation even though they are recognized as such by every survey which has been made to date. When the Minister of Industry introduced the new program on August 5, 1965 he said the areas which qualify are characterized by high and chronic unemployment, low family incomes, and contain some 16 per cent of the national labour force as compared with approximately 7.5 per cent of the labour force covered under the former plan.
There is low unemployment in the area concerned because there is no industrial expansion. There has been an industrial decline and an industrial stagnation. The employees have moved away to become unemployment statistics in the metropolitan centres. The government boasts of policies to relieve unemployment but they have done so at the expense of rural areas. The workers have migrated to metropolitan centres but they want to return to their homes in the Georgian bay and lake Huron areas.
These problems have been of great concern to myself and to my colleague, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce. We have communicated with the Minister of Industry, but with no success. There have been numerous delegations and representations made to the department but to no avail. We have made every possible approach to the department concerned. We have joined with representatives of the communities concerned, with county councils, industrial commissions, chambers of commerce and individual businessmen. We have used a non-political approach. We have had delegates from the Liberal organizations, and on one occasion a delegation which had among its members the defeated Liberal candidates from that region. That was a large delegation.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce and myself are concerned about the future of our area. I may assure the house that we are not alone in this concern. The provincial member for Bruce, a member of the Liberal party, is also very much concerned. He is especially concerned abou a commitment made to the
July 11. 1966

people of Kincardine on November 4 prior to the last election.
I am now referring to a letter written by that member to the Prime Minister on May 19, 1966. The letter was published in an article headed "Ross Whicher Requests Action on Recent Federal Election Promise by Liberal Party". It was written at the Parliament Buildings, Queen's Park, Toronto, Ont., and reads as follows:
The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson Prime Minister of Canada House of Commons Ottawa. Canada My Dear Prime Minister:
During the past several weeks I have written to you twice in regard to the statement issued immediately previous to the last federal election by the Liberal candidate for Bruce in so far as the town of Kincardine and its immediate area were to be affected by the term "designated area" is concerned. I have also talked to your secretary by telephone and had correspondence with the Hon. Mr. Drury, the Minister in charge of this particular problem.
I will not go into the question again as to whether Kincardine should or should not be included as a designated area. There are arguments on both sides. However, to me as the Liberal member for the area for the past eleven years in the provincial legislature, there is a far more serious question. It is a matter to me of principle and of honour. May I quote the News Release that was given verbally to the people of Kincardine by Kent Lamont, the Liberal candidate, just a few days before the last election, and also given to the press, radio and television.
Statement received by Gordon Beaton from Mr. Keith Davey this afternoon, November 4th, by phone to be conveyed to Mr. Kent Lamont, Liberal candidate in the riding of Bruce re designated areas. If Mr. Lamont wishes to make a statement publicly the following is the suggested announcement he should make: "I have been in touch with the Minister of Industry who has advised me that the area development agency of his department have embarked upon a study to determine what should be the boundaries of the Georgian Bay economic region. They are being assisted in this study by the Ontario government." If Mr. Lamont wishes he could add the following: "I have been authorized that I may announce that Kincardine area will after this study be included in the area already designated. I have been assured by the Minister that circumstances in the Kincardine area are exactly that which these studies are directed and that I can assure the people of the Kincardine area that it will be included in the designated area."
Can anything be more explicit? Here we have the word of Keith Davey, now a Senator who, at that time was national organizer for the Liberal party and through his position speaking officially for the Liberal party.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
This promise has not been kept. Honour has been a word that has been synonymous with your whole life. May I respectfully say that it is a word that has described your political life more than any other. I hope that in a small way it helps to describe me. Most humbly I tell you that I did
Interim Supply
not win this riding against such Conservative leadership as Leslie Frost and John Robarts by stretching the truth even in an election campaign. And by our lack of action we Liberals have certainly misinformed the people of Kincardine. Out of respect for my Prime Minister I am being temperate in my wording. If you were an ordinary Liberal I would use that language which I normally employ to describe such things.
He concludes by saying:
Under the circumstances, as outlined above, it will be impossible for me to associate myself with any proclamations or declarations that your government may issue for this area. Regrettably, I would always have the feeling that it might not be carried out.
Yours very truly,
Ross M. Whicher, M.P.P.
(Bruce)
I ask the government to honour their pledge. Again I ask the government to alleviate the serious situation which exists today. The designated areas program provides for an annual review. Has this problem been reconsidered? I do not want action of the kind described by the minister when pressed to remove the discrimination and competition created by this bill, namely to remove designation from the adjacent area. Unemployment is the basic criterion for designation, yet the word "unemployment" appears only once in the statement of the minister extending over some five pages, which he made on August 5, 1965.
With reference to that statement, Mr. Chairman, I say that that word was used only once. He went on to use very descriptive phrases, such as economic difficulties, variety of industries, growing markets, industrial development, economic growth, employment opportunities and incentive program. When the Prime Minister introduced this legislation first on June 7, 1965, he indicated that the program of incentives for area development was a further measure in the government's campaign against poverty and inadequate opportunities, and as reported at page 2022 of Hansard he said:
This program is designed to encourage the establishment of industry in areas of Canada where there is a special need to raise employment and income and broaden economic opportunity for people.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I submit that if the people of my riding do not qualify for this, then I do not know what they would qualify for.
With regard to the minister's statement, I would ask, why such narrow criteria for such a broad program of assistance? I recognize that statistical criteria must be employed, but we have asked that designation apply to the

July 11. 1966
Interim Supply
general area on a regional basis or on a county basis, or counties adjacent to one another having similar problems and need for special economic development incentives. I ask not only for designation of the area in my riding but also for designation on a regional basis, so that general economic conditions will be improved and development accelerated.
In support of my plea this evening I should like to refer to the letter I received from the mayor of Kincardine this afternoon. It is dated July 9, 1966 and is as follows:
Dear Sir:
I follow very closely all reports from parliament as given by the London Free Press. I appreciate and wish to express my personal thanks for your efforts on our behalf re designated area. I note you are bringing attention to a letter by Ross Whicher to the Prime Minister on our behalf before the house next week. I personally wrote the Prime Minister on June 9, 1966 re statements by Kent Lamont, also a reply to a telegram from the Prime Minister after our delegation to Ottawa last summer and I am also waiting for a reply.
I also had a telephone call this evening from the chairman of the industrial commission in Kincardine, who received a copy of the statement alleged to have been circulated by the Liberal organization-and I say alleged because I have no way of knowing whether or not it is authentic until the government takes some sort of action. This is the statement that was forwarded, in the first instance, to the candidates in the last campaign. In his telephone conversation this evening the chairman urged me to do everything possible to alleviate the serious situation existing today in the town of Kincardine. He pointed to the area immediately to the north, which has already benefited from the designation; and while I do not doubt for one moment that there is a certain amount of jealousy, I feel that the people in the area are quite justified in feeling that way when we read that there has been recent industrial expansion and development in the communities which are immediately affected, namely Port Elgin, Owen Sound, Midland and further north.
Just recently there has been a new $1 million plant which commenced construction in the town of Port Elgin. There must be something wrong in the area, Mr. Chairman, when the Prime Minister chooses the Bruce peninsula, in particular the city of Owen Sound, to announce on November 4 tax incentives which were designed to help the tourist industry to earn more U.S. dollars. This announcement was featured in an article in the Globe and Mail for that date under the heading "P.M. announces incentives".

There must be something wrong when we see press clippings on June 29, particularly one in the Port Elgin Times, which says that this area has been selected for a job vacancy survey.
There must be something wrong, Mr. Chairman, when a Liberal candidate prior to the last election said that, if elected, he would attempt to have the riding of Grey-Bruce designated in order to receive assistance to secure new industries. Another candidate in the riding of Bruce referred to the fact that action in Bruce county was needed, and this, mind you, is after the program had been brought in on August 5, 1965.
Another press clipping, this time from the Kincardine News for December 15, 1965, is headed "Confer with federal Minister of Inquiry" and commences as follows:
The exclusion of the Kincardine area from the federal government's "designated area" has dealt a severe blow to any hopes of attracting industry to this region, but the members of the local Industrial Committee are still striving to change the decision to draw the boundary line at North Bruce.
Another editorial is headed "Discrimination in Designated Areas".
We ask, Mr. Chairman, that something be done to alleviate this situation. We ask for consideration. We ask further for some amendment of the act to be brought in to equate opportunities in the Georgian Bay area. We ask that something-anything-be done to rectify the current decline and regression. Surely, Mr. Chairman, even though this government has a record of so many changes, revisions, last minute stands and reversals, it will find that in changing the formula it would not be setting any unwarranted precedent.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I regret having to take a couple moments of the time of this committee, but there are certain things that I must bring to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is responsible, of course, for the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and for the recent so-called baby census that has taken place.
This variety of census of course is very important, and it should be accurate because government policies having to do with social welfare, immigration, finance and the like are dependant on its accuracy, as are businesses and like institutions throughout the country. A couple of instances of inaccuracies in the
July 11, 1966



recent census have been brought to my attention. I am sure that other hon. members have had similar things brought to their attention.
This census, Mr. Chairman, has cost many millions of dollars. Many government departments and government policies are dependant on the accuracy of it. I should like to cite an instance of inaccuracy in the census, for the benefit of the minister, and I hope that he may send out instructions, or that he may request the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to sent out instructions, so that something can be done to rectify the obvious mistakes and inaccuracies which have crept into the recent census taking.
A newspaper in the city of Woodstock reports an astonishing incident where a census taker went to a residence in which there are a number of apartments. The census taker, apparently unable to find at home some of the persons living in the apartment house requested the proprietor of the building to guess at the answers to some of the six questions that were put. The proprietor declined the invitation, and presumably the census taker filled in the answers from his, or her, as the case may be, imagination. It turned out that one of the occupants of the apartment building had been enumerated without her knowledge, and it was quite clear therefore that the information must have been filled in from the imagination of the census taker.
Another incident brought to my attention was in the city of Toronto. The home of a relation of mine, who at the time was temporarily absent was enumerated; Also his daughter, a university student, was taking a course outside the country. It turns out that the person replying to the census taker was informed that since two persons were absent from the residence on the day of enumeration, they could not be included in the census. Incidentally the hon. member for York South was informed of this incident by letter.
The thing I was to bring to the minister's attention is this: One of these incidents was uncovered by a newspaper, and the other was brought to my attention by a private individual, These are two instances of inaccuracies. There must be many other inaccuracies in this census. Even if 1 per cent of the information is wrong, that could have a very serious effect on the results of the census and the use to which the figures arising from it can be put.
This census has cost the taxpayers many millions of dollars. I hope that the Minister of
Ways and Means
Trade and Commerce considers it his responsibility to see that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics checks into this matter, to see if anything can be done about remedying these inaccuracies. It is quite clear, Mr. Chairman, that those who were responsible for instructing the census takers did not do their jobs very well. As for the people taking the census, certainly a considerable number of them did not know what they were doing.
I draw this to the minister's attention and I hope that he may take the appropriate remedial action.

Motion agreed to.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Batten in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to have the attention of the Minister of National Revenue for just a few moments with regard to a matter that I have had occasion to raise many times. The references that I wish to make on this occasion, however, are few and brief.
On June 17, as recorded in Hansard at page 6543, I asked the Minister of National Revenue if he would consider arranging for a term of reference to be given to the joint committee on the public service so that it might discuss the question of, adjusting the pensions of retired civil servants. The minister replied on that occasion in these words:

Mr. Speaker, I certainly would have no objection to doing that providing the committee completes the huge amount of work it now has before it in considering four very complicated bills.
I replied:
That is fine: we can do it after we have completed the other bills.
Ten days later, as recorded in Hansard at page 6873, I renewed the question. On that occasion I asked the minister if he would discuss with representatives of the various parties in the house the possible wording of a

July 11. 1966
Ways and Means
term of reference so that the matter of increasing the pensions of retired civil servants might be considered by the joint committee on the public service when it has finished the other matters that have been referred to it.
I should like to read the reply given on that occasion, which as I have said is on page 6873. It reads as follows:

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as soon as the joint committee has dealt with the rather tremendous task it has in front of it, namely the consideration of the bills to implement collective bargaining in the civil service, I would be pleased to discuss such a resolution with representative members of the parties opposite as well as with my cabinet colleagues, whose approval I must obtain before putting such a resolution on the order paper.
At no point in these proceedings have I attempted to get out of the minister more than I feel he promised. He made it very clear that the subject matter of my request, namely for the joint committee on the public service to discuss the pensions of retired civil servants, would have to come after we have considered the four bills referred to it. We have finished one of them, namely, the pension integration bill. The other three bills relate to the question of collective bargaining in the civil service and they are still before that committee.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
It will obviously take some weeks, it may be fall, before we complete the work on the collective bargaining in the civil service, but it was my hope that the minister might meet the suggestion I made on June 27, namely that an appropriate term of reference might be drafted in order that those who are interested might know that this important question will be discussed by that committee.
The reason I suggested to the minister that he might discuss the wording of the term of reference with representatives of the various parties is that usually when something is done this way there is no debate on the floor of this house on such a motion. If there were an all-party agreement on such a term of reference it could be brought before the house some night just before closing time; it could be passed and then those who are interested would know that pensions of retired civil servants would be discussed in the committee.
I do not suggest, when I say this, that there is any question about the minister's promise. He is a man of his word. But I should be glad if before the recess, which will come along

one of these days, he would confirm that this matter of pensions paid to retired civil servants and their widows can and will be discussed by the joint committee when it has finished its consideration of the other three bills.

I would simply say that I stand behind everything I have said in this respect. I personally have no objection to this matter going to the committee when it has completed the considerable amount of work presently before it. At the time I first answered the hon. member on this point there were four bills to be dealt with. Indeed I would hope that when we have completed supply we could quickly move to discuss item 51 on the order paper, so that we might have three items open. But when those three important measures have been disposed of, namely the bill with respect to collective bargaining in the public service, the Financial Administration Act and the new public service act, I would certainly be most pleased to see that the matter of which the hon. member has spoken is brought before the committee.
I do not believe I can give any further assurance than this-the assurance that I personally would like to see this matter discussed when the other important and urgent matters have been cleared up. However, as I stated earlier, I am not committing the government. I am merely saying that I personally am in favour of having this question discussed, and I leave the matter open.

I thank the minister for his words of confirmation. He has stated his own position as a minister with respect to this matter and I dare to believe, and I dare to hope, that his cabinet colleagues will back him up when the time comes.
With respect to his suggestion that in a moment or two we might deal with order 51, I am sure we would all agree to that. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-215, respecting certain conditions of employment of dock workers at the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I can think of no better way to introduce the motion that this bill be read a second time than to read the preamble to it:
Whereas the processes of free collective bargaining and of mediation between representatives of employing shipping companies using the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec and of dock workers at those ports have been successful in producing agreement on wages and most of the other issues in dispute at the time of the strike of such dock workers that began in the month of May, 1966, and, in the report of the mediator appointed to mediate the issues then in dispute, it was recommended that an industrial inquiry commission be appointed under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to inquire into certain matters on which agreement was not reached and to report its conclusions thereon to the Minister of Labour at the earliest possible date;
And whereas an industrial inquiry commission to inquire into those certain matters has been appointed under the said act, and it is in the national interest that the conclusions of the said commission with respect thereto be carried into effect without delay following receipt of the report of the said commission, by the incorporation of those conclusions in the terms of settlement that were entered into following the settlement of the other issues involved in the dispute and in any collective agreements entered into pursuant to those terms of settlement.
The collective agreement under which the dock workers at the three ports worked for a period of nearly three years prior to May of this year, actually expired on December 31, 1965. Prior to its expiration, in fact in late October of last year, the unions concerned

served notice of their intention to insist on changes in the agreement when the time came to negotiate.
It is of some significance that other locals of the International Longshoremen's Association represent the dock workers in the cities of Halifax and Saint John. The traffic on the St. Lawrence being closed in the early part of 1966, and the Port of Halifax being open, the Shipping Federation of Canada agreed with the Halifax local on the terms of a new collective agreement, and negotiations were opened with the bargaining representatives of the local in Saint John, New Brunswick. The new Halifax agreement provides that members of that union will receive any greater benefits that may be given to the St. Lawrence ports members as a result of subsequent negotiations.
On or about January 31 of this year the International Longshoremen's Association made application on behalf of the unions in the three St. Lawrence ports for the appointment of a conciliation officer to mediate their disputes. A series of meetings, upwards of 20 in number, took place between the bargaining representatives of the locals in the three ports and the shipping federation.
These meetings began in or about the early part of February and they continued well into the month of March. A long list of requests was presented by the longshoremen's association. Some counter proposals were submitted by the shipping federation. At these 20 odd meetings that were held in February and March several, though not all of these issues were discussed at some length, and I might say that the requests involved both monetary and non-monetary items.
About the end of March, following the breakdown of negotiations between the parties, the unions made application to me as Minister of Labour for conciliation services, and on April 4 I appointed a conciliator to mediate the matters in dispute. On April 15 the conciliation officer reported to me by telegram that there was considerable unrest in the port of Montreal, and that there was the likelihood of a wildcat strike. He recommended that a conciliation board be established immediately.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
On the same day, April 15, I established a board as requested. The parties were notified by telegram of this fact and were asked to nominate their representative member to the board. Four days later a wildcat strike took place in the Port of Montreal, ostensibly over
July 11, 1966



the automobile parking privileges granted the longshoremen at that port. In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I might say that there probably were other reasons such as the delay factor in making progress with the negotiations. In any event the wildcat strike did occur. I asked Mr. Poirier, the conciliation officer, to intervene to see what he could do to have the men return to work.
In the meantime, on April 20 the Shipping Federation nominated its member on the conciliation board. On April 25 the International Longshoremen's Association nominated its representative on the board. In the meantime partly through the good offices of the conciliation officer, the men had returned to work on April 21. On April 29, the two representative members were formally appointed as members of the board and they were asked to agree on the third member who would be chairman.
On May 10, some 12 days later, the representatives of the two parties, the longshoremen's association and the shipping federation, agreed upon Mr. Justice Claude Prevost as the third member and chairman. On that same day a second illegal or wildcat strike occured at the Port of Montreal. The shipping federation then took the position that the union members should call off the illegal strike as a condition precedent to the continuation of the conciliation proceedings.
Hon. members will recall that at that time I expressed concern over this situation and actually expressed disapproval of the action of the federation, since I thought it was important that the conciliation board should proceed with a minimum of delay. I think I should reiterate, because of the tense situation which developed, that just prior to establishment of this conciliation board with a conciliation officer on the job-he had been there about two weeks-a walkout or illegal strike had occurred and the men had returned to work on April 31, only to walk out again on May 10. I mention these walkouts because they added to the tension and helped create a very difficult atmosphere for any conciliation or mediation proceedings.
I am not saying where the fault lay; usually there is fault on both sides in cases of that kind. Whatever the reason, because of the attitudes of the parties the conciliation board was not able to deal with any of the issues in dispute. They heard no evidence of any kind, no representations, and so reported to me on May 17. On the following day, May 18, I appointed His Honour Judge Rene Lippe,
Labour Conditions
chairman of the trustees of the Maritime Transportation Association, as a mediator in this dispute. I think as every member in this house knows Judge Lippe is an experienced and able administrator with a broad experience in labour-management disputes.
I appealed to both parties to get together with Judge Lippe with a view to working out a settlement of the issues. He held several meetings with the parties during the period May 18 to June 13 inclusive, During this period he submitted several interim reports to me, some of which I passed on to the house. His final report was submitted to me on June 23 and this report was tabled by my parliamentary secretary on July 4.
As pointed out in the mediator's report, in the final stages of negotiation the crucial issues in the dispute were the size of the wage increase, job security, calls and recalls on the one hand and increased productivity and related matters on the other. From meetings which took place in Ottawa during the later stages of negotiation, June 10, 11, 12 and 13, it was obvious to everyone who had given serious tnought to the matter that it would be absolutely impossible to get the shipping federation to agree to the very substantial increases in wages for 1966 and 1967, and the other benefits requested by the union, without assurance to them that they might expect some increased productivity at least during the year 1967.
In the early stages of negotiation the shipping federation had admitted that they were prepared to forgo any increase during 1966, but they thought that if they were going to be asked for further substantial increases to take effect in 1967, there should be some assurance of increased productivity in return.
I think I can summarize the position of the shipping federation by saying they simply were not prepared to agree to any increases for the second year without some assurance of increased productivity during the latter part of the two year term. I might refer to one of the documents that was tabled by me on Friday last. It is headed Terms of Settlement for the Two-Year Collective Agreement between the International Longshoremen's locals in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres, Quebec and The Shipping Federation of Canada. The first paragraph of the agreement reads:
1. Each employee will receive 40c. for every hour worked as of January 1, 1966, made up as follows:-
20c. increase per man-hour worked retroactive to January 1, 1966, and effective up to but not including the day work resumes; and

July 11, 1966
Labour Conditions
20c. per man-hour worked retroactive to January 1, 1966, effective up to but not including the day work resumes, in compensation for improvements in productivity.
From date of resumption of work the above increases shall be applied on overtime as well.
That is, there would be no increase on the overtime prior to the date of resumption of work. Paragraph 2. has a similar provision:
An additional 15c. per hour increase in wages to be effective January 1, 1967; and a further 25c. per hour increase in wages to be effective on May 1, 1967 also in compensation for improvements in productivity. These increases shall be applied on overtime as well.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In the interests of brevity, it might be well for me to refer to the report of the mediator, which hon. members have had the opportunity to peruse, since I filed it in this house a week ago. On page 2 the mediator reports as follows:
Basically, the request of the association was:
(A)	A 50 cents hourly increase retroactive to January 1st 1966;
(B)	A further hourly increase of 50 cents for the year 1967;
(C)	No modification of the work load until at the earliest January 1st 1968.
In addition, there was presented by the association a long list of further requests which, for the purpose of brevity I will qualify as fringe benefits, although this expression is not perfect in this instance. These requests were both of a monetary and of a non-monetary nature.
On the other hand, the stand of the Federation was that they are engaged in a competitive business and that any labour contract must take into consideration the economics of the business. In that light, the Federation stated that they were not in a position to make an offer as to the hourly wages and other benefits unless and until the question of the work load has been determined. Reference was made at that time by the Federation to the contract entered into in Halifax between the I.L.A. Longshoremen local and the Federation.
It was easy to determine on that first day that the parties were really too far apart to reach an agreement. I, therefore, decided to meet with the parties separately in an effort to mediate the issues for the immediate future, leaving for further negotiations a long term contract which would expire in 1968, if not 1969.
These meetings of the commissioner with each of the parties took place daily until Saturady the 21st, mclusive, at which time I submitted to the parties the following recommendations:-
I will not go into the details of the next two and a half pages of the report, but I should like to say that the mediator submitted to both sides these recommendations since the shipping federation was prepared to agree to a substantial increase in 1966 but not to a further increase in 1967. He suggested that the unions accept the

increase which he proposed for 1966 and that an industrial inquiry commission be set up immediately to look into the matter of uroductivity and related matters. The parties would then have the benefit of this report, and he felt that within a relatively short time, certainly before the end of the year, these matters could be subjects for a negotiated contract for 1967-68 or possibly 1967, 1968 and 1969.
The mediator, continuing with his report at page 5 said:
Owing to the urgence of the situation, it has been impossible for the undersigned to give proper consideration to the question of reduction of crews. However, because of the importance of this issue, the undersigned recommends as soon as possible the appointment by the Minister of Labour of the government of Canada of an industrial inquiry commission to study this problem.
Without criticizing the past conduct of either party, the undersigned, pursuant to discussions with said parties, is of the opinion that it would be desirable that negotiations relative to the next collective agreement be initiated immediately.
The industrial inquiry commission who will study the problem of reduction in crews could also deal with this problem of negotiations.
This passage refers to wages and fringe benefits accompanying reorganization and improvements. This proposal was submitted to the shipping federation and to the unions but the unions did not accept it. In fact, their officers did not recommend it and they gave as one of their reasons that they did not want the contract to expire on December 31, 1966 only to find themselves in the midst of another serious dispute in the year of our centennial.
The union leaders told me that out of respect for the mediator they did call a meeting and submitted the proposal. They did not recommend it, however, and it was turned down. That was the proposal for the interim settlement for the year 1966 only. I might say that this recommendation for an interim solution was accepted by the shipping federation.
This turn down took place on Tuesday, the 25th, at the mass meeting, and the association rejected the mediator's recommendation for a temporary settlement. On Wednesday, the 25th, the parties were requested by telegram to meet again with the mediator. This they did and on that occasion the President of the International Longshoremen's Union from New York, Mr. T. W. Gleason, came to Montreal and met with the mediator and the representatives of the union. There was a caucus held of the shipping federation members and they made a further offer which is set out at pages 7 and 8 of the mediator's
July 11, 1966

report. I am not going to go into detail on it because it was not accepted.
On May 26 the unions made an offer which they referred to as their minimum proposals. There was some reduction in what they asked for. Instead of asking for 50 cents an hour in 1966 and another 50 cents an hour in 1967 they agreed to accept 40 cents an hour in 1966 and a further 40 cents an hour in 1967. These were the basic increases in the hourly rates, although there were fringe benefits and other items involved.
On May 27 that proposal was submitted to the shipping federation. On the following morning the shipping federation said it would not accept this proposal and again reiterated its stand with respect to a definite assurance that in the second year there had to be some assurance of increased productivity. At that time the mediator got in touch with me and presented one of his interim reports. He suggested that I invite representatives of both sides to Ottawa to discuss the basic provisions, and explore the possibility of settlement on the strength of an assurance that an industrial inquiry commission would be set up to inquire into the crucial issues. He indicated that such a course might lead to a settlement.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
As I have already advised the house on an earlier occasion, in company with two of my colleagues, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau), and my deputy minister I met with the representatives of both parties here, and their legal advisers, in the later afternoon of May 27. Extended discussions took place. The memorandum used as a basis for such discussions contained the minimum demands put forward by the longshoremen on May 26.
On that occasion I suggested to the two parties that since it seemed that agreement was possible on most of the issues-I would say over 40 of the 50-odd issues that were involved-and agreement seemed almost certain on all but perhaps five or six of these items, they might agree to establish an independent commission and they could choose their own commissioner to inquire into the possibilities of increased productivity and related matters. I will not go into detail, but in the course of the discussion arguments were put forward that the average crew, or gang, strength in the port of Montreal is 18-I refer, of course, to a longshoremen's gang-but in Trois-Rivieres it is 16, in Halifax it is 16,
Labour Conditions
in Toronto it is 15 and on the west coast, in Vancouver and other ports, I am told that it is substantially less than that.
The longshoremen were concerned with job security and said it would have to be shown conclusively, or beyond a reasonable doubt, that they were not going to suffer through some whim on the part of the employers; it would have to be established. So my suggestion was that this inquiry commission could hear the evidence of both sides. The commissioner would be whom they would agree upon, or if they could not agree on one I, as Minister of Labour, after getting their advice would appoint one, that each side would have an assessor who would be there to assist the commissioner, and he could have as long as he felt necessary to inquire into the situation.
I might say that at this time, in the early morning of May 28, there was no suggestion of any legislative enactment to make the findings of the commission binding. The suggestion was that this be a voluntary arrangement between the two parties. Discussions lasted several hours and we adjourned in the wee, small hours of Saturday, May 28. The next morning the representative of the longshoremen got in touch with me and said, "I am not saying we will agree"

to the appointment of such a commission-"but there would be no point in our agreeing to it if the employers are not going to come along and meet what we refer to as the balance of our minimum terms". I said that I would speak to the employers, if he would discuss it with his people. This was on Saturday. We met the following day in Montreal. My colleague the Minister of Industry and my parliamentary secretary were with me. We had interesting, useful meetings. There is no doubt that there was a considerable narrowing of the issues, but the negotiations broke down again in the wee, small hours of Monday the 30th, this time largely on the issue of job security.
The international vice president of the longshoremen's association said that he was concerned with job security; he was not so much concerned with an inquiry. There might be an inquiry, there might not be; but he did not want the employers taking a position that was going to throw out of work bona fide longshoremen who had worked for an appreciable length of time. There were arguments about university students, taxi drivers and others who might not be bona fide longshoremen. In the course of the next day or two these points were straightened out by an exchange of wires; but when the

July 11. 1966
Labour Conditions
mediator brought the parties together again in late May-or it might have been early June-the unions then stated that they could not go along with the proposal for a commission. They made their position clear; they said, "If the government wants to establish a commission, it can." Other alternatives were explored by the mediator and, as shown in his report, on about June 10 or 11 he got in touch with me again and suggested another meeting in Ottawa.
This time they came to Ottawa on Saturday, June 11. My colleagues the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), who had an interest in this matter because of the harbour board docks in Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), who had had a broad experience in this field, the President of the Privy Council, my deputy minister and I met with the two sides.
The first meeting began in the middle of the morning. It was then said, according to the report-the mediator was there-that apparently a deadlock or an impasse had occurred. I then invited suggestions for a solution and made the statement that the issues could not stay deadlocked forever. Then I made the suggestion, which had actually originated with the mediator, that consideration might be given, if they could agree on every other point except increased productivity and job security, to refer those issues to the commissioner.
At the meeting on the morning of Saturday, June 11, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Jodoin, was present and in the course of the meeting not only I but my colleague the Minister of Transport- at least the two of us-said, "It looks as if there might be a solution if we were to establish a commission and agree that its findings might be made binding on these two points."

speechtext: May I ask the minister a very short question? I assume he is speaking about Mr. Cutler. In reply to a question by the minister as to what the association would do if such legislation were passed, Mr. Cutler said they would obey the law; is that what happened?

speechtext: I think I mentioned earlier that both Mr. Pickersgill and I had invited the longshoremen to speak quite freely. I might say that the shipping federation was not there. We asked if the longshoremen had any suggestions to make. Naturally they would have liked a contract continuing through to January 1, 1968 with an extra 40 cents next year and without any commitments on a change in productivity. There is no doubt about that phase of it in the early stages. However, when we asked them to bring forward any suggestions they might have, and they were not forthcoming, there were two occasions at which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and I said that it had been suggested we establish the commission and that we might make only the findings on these issues binding. I will not say we took it as acquiescence at first, because the discussions continued for another 14 hours. There were further discussions in the afternoon during which there was no doubt as to their acquiescence to certain aspects of the proposal.
After the morning meeting we met again in the West Block, this time with simultaneous interpretation so that any of the longshoremen, who might not understand me, because my French is far from fluent, would know what I and others, said in the course of the discussions. I might say that the president of the Canadian Labour Congress said again that the congress was opposed to compulsory arbitration and that he wanted to make that fact clear.
The question was again asked, this time by Mr. Pickersgill, whether there was any other solution. We left the morning meeting at about 1.30 p.m. to meet with the shipping federation with whom we spent several hours in the afternoon. They insisted that an agreement be reached for the reorganization of longshoremen's gangs, new types of slings and other changes that might result in increased productivity. Eventually they did agree that if the government would take the responsibility for setting up the commission and agree to pass legislation, they would acquiesce in such a course and would agree to the second payment of 40 cents in 1967; 15 cents were paid on January 1 and 25 cents later in the year when the recommendations of the commission were implemented.
Other points were discussed at that meeting at which my colleagues and I, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Transport, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) and my deputy minister were present. Approved revised report of federal-provincial standing committee on concept OF STUDENTS' NEEDS
The premises on which the concepts of need are based include the following:
(a)	The responsibility for the costs of postsecondary education to the individual student remains primarily with the parent (guardian or immediate family) and/orthe student.
(b)	Government at all levels are interested in supplementing family-student resources and resources available through educational institutions, where needed to ensure that all qualified students have the opportunity to reach their educational potential.
(c)	It is desirable that the concepts and criteria used by governments and institutions in determining the need for loans, bursaries and other forms of assistance to students should be co-ordinated within a province by a provincial authority.
(d)	It is desirable to co-ordinate among the provinces the concepts and criteria of need applied in administering federal assistance in this field.
2.	Both the costs of education and the resources available to the student should be taken into account in developing the concepts of need.
The following criteria should be employed:
A.	COSTS OF EDUCATION
The following costs should be taken into account in determining need:
(1)	Fees-All compulsory fees of the educational institution.
(2)	Prescribed Books and Instruments.
(3)	Board and Lodging During the Academic Year.
(i)	Institutional Residence-as charged by the institution.
(ii)	Board and lodging away from home based on average costs in the region concerned.
(iii)	Students living at home will be given a cost allowance of 40-50% of the costs allowed for board and lodging for students living away from home.
(4)	A Reasonable Allowance for Clothing, Laundry, Dry-Cleaning and Recreational Cost.
(5)	Transportation.
(a)	From permanent residence in Canada to institution in Canada-
Two return trips a year, the cost not to exceed the equivalent of the cost of the most economical means based on costs of public transportation.
(b)	From permanent residence in Canada to institution outside of Canada-
An allowance which will equal the lesser of one return trip a year by the most economical transportation, or a maximum amount established by the provinces.
(c)	A Reasonable Allowance for Local Transportation.
(6)	Premiums for Hospital and Medical Prepayment Plans.
B.	RESOURCES TO MEET COSTS OF EDUCATION
(1)	Resources of Parents/Guardian of Dependent Students
A single student engaged in post-secondary education below the first university degree and who has not been previously financially independent through employment for a period of at least one year is to be defined as being dependent.
Parents' income and assets are to be taken into account.
All application forms will have sections which elicit information concerning the parents' gross income, including for selfemployed people gross income and expenses of a business or farm, and in all cases a statement of assets and liabilities.
(2)	Students' Own Resources
(a)	Summer Earnings
(b)	All Assets
(i)	Car (state value)
(ii)	Other assets
(c)	Earnings During the Academic Year
(d)	Scholarships, Bursaries and Tuition Grants
(3)	Married Students' Resources
The resources of a married student shall be the income available to that married student and his spouse less a predetermined annual allowance for basic family maintenance costs, depending on the size of the family, less the board and lodging allowances referred to in A (3) (iii) above.

3.	General Recommendations
(1)	Where an applicant feels that the award is inadequate or circumstances have changed since the award was made, the applicant may either appeal his case or re-apply to the provincial authority or to an institution delegated by that authority in accordance with the procedure established by the province concerned.
(2)	A declaration shall be made in the application by the student, and where applicable by the parent or guardian, knowing it to be of the same force and effect as if made under oath by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
(3)	These premises and criteria are acceptable to provincial and federal governments, and the federal and all provincial authorities
will co-operate in giving full publicity to them.
4.	Continuing attention will be given to developing a common application form for use in the provinces.
